#132440. Tech Report: Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

📅 09 Feb 2022 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2888 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ieee ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

📅 09 Feb 2022 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2888 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The AI pioneer notes it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to big challenges.
  • Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.
  • Sources indicate that andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The AI pioneer notes it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to big challenges.

Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.

Sources indicate that andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence. He pioneered the use of graphics processing units (GPUs) to train deep learning models in the late 2000s with his students at Stanford University, cofounded Google Brain in 2011, and then served for three years as chief scientist for Baidu, where he helped build the Chinese tech giant’s AI group. So when he claims he has identified the next significant shift in artificial intelligence, people listen. And that’s what he told IEEE Spectrum in an exclusive Q&A.

Ng’s current efforts are focused on his manufacturer Landing AI, which built a platform called LandingLens to help manufacturers improve visual inspection with computer vision. He has also become something of an evangelist for what he calls the data-centric AI movement, which he indicates can yield “small data” solutions to big issues in AI, including model efficiency, accuracy, and bias.

Industry observers note that the great advances in deep learning over the past decade or so have been powered by ever-bigger models crunching ever-bigger amounts of data. Some people argue that that’s an unsustainable trajectory. Do you agree that it can’t go on that way?

According to recent reports, andrew Ng: This is a big question. We’ve seen foundation models in NLP [natural language processing]. I’m excited about NLP models getting even bigger, and also about the potential of building foundation models in computer vision. I think there’s lots of signal to still be exploited in video: We have not been able to build foundation models yet for video because of compute bandwidth and the cost of processing video, as opposed to tokenized text. So I think that this engine of scaling up deep learning algorithms, which has been running for something like 15 years now, still has steam in it. Having stated that, it only applies to certain problems, and there’s a set of other problems that need small data solutions.

When you say you want a foundation model for computer vision, what do you mean by that?

Ng: This is a term coined by Percy Liang and some of my friends at Stanford to refer to very large models, trained on very large data sets, that can be tuned for specific applications. For example, GPT-3 is an example of a foundation model [for NLP]. Foundation models offer a lot of promise as a new paradigm in developing machine learning applications, but also challenges in terms of making sure that they’re reasonably fair and free from bias, especially if many of us will be building on top of them.

What needs to happen for someone to build a foundation model for video?

Industry observers note that ng: I think there is a scalability problem. The compute power needed to process the large volume of images for video is significant, and I think that’s why foundation models have arisen first in NLP. Many researchers are working on this, and I think we’re seeing early signs of such models being developed in computer vision. But I’m confident that if a semiconductor maker gave us 10 times more processor power, we could easily find 10 times more video to build such models for vision.

Sources indicate that having remarked that, a lot of what’s happened over the past decade is that deep learning has happened in consumer-facing companies that have large user bases, sometimes billions of owners, and therefore very large data sets. While that paradigm of machine learning has driven a lot of economic value in consumer software, I find that that recipe of scale doesn’t work for other industries.

It’s funny to hear you say that, because your early work was at a consumer-facing company with millions of owners.

Recent findings suggest that ng: Over a decade ago, when I proposed starting the Google Brain project to use Google’s compute infrastructure to build very large neural networks, it was a controversial step. One very senior person pulled me aside and warned me that starting Google Brain would be bad for my career. I think he felt that the action couldn’t just be in scaling up, and that I should instead focus on architecture innovation.

“In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from significant data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.” —Andrew Ng, CEO & Founder, Landing AI.

I remember when my students and I published the first NeurIPS workshop paper advocating using CUDA, a platform for processing on GPUs, for deep learning—a different senior person in AI sat me down and said, “CUDA is really complicated to program. As a programming paradigm, this seems like too much work.” I did manage to convince him; the other person I did not convince.

I expect they’re both convinced now.

In a recent development, over the past year as I’ve been speaking to people about the data-centric AI movement, I’ve been getting flashbacks to when I was speaking to people about deep learning and scalability 10 or 15 years ago. In the past year, I’ve been getting the same mix of “there’s nothing newly introduced here” and “this seems like the wrong direction.”.

How do you define data-centric AI, and why do you consider it a movement?

In a recent development, ng: Data-centric AI is the discipline of systematically engineering the data needed to successfully build an AI system. For an AI system, you have to implement some algorithm, say a neural network, in code and then train it on your data set. The dominant paradigm over the last decade was to download the data set while you focus on improving the code. Thanks to that paradigm, over the last decade deep learning networks have improved significantly, to the point where for a lot of applications the code—the neural network architecture—is basically a solved problem. So for many practical applications, it’s now more productive to hold the neural network architecture fixed, and instead find ways to improve the data.

When I started speaking about this, there were many practitioners who, completely appropriately, raised their hands and noted, “Yes, we’ve been doing this for 20 years.” This is the time to take the things that some individuals have been doing intuitively and make it a systematic engineering discipline.

The data-centric AI movement is much bigger than one manufacturer or group of researchers. My collaborators and I organized a data-centric AI workshop at NeurIPS, and I was really delighted at the number of authors and presenters that showed up.

Industry observers note that you often talk about companies or institutions that have only a small amount of data to work with. How can data-centric AI help them?

It has been revealed that ng: You hear a lot about vision systems built with millions of images—I once built a face recognition system using 350 million images. Architectures built for hundreds of millions of images don’t work with only 50 images. But it turns out, if you have 50 really good examples, you can build something valuable, like a defect-inspection system. In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from substantial data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.

When you talk about training a model with just 50 images, does that really mean you’re taking an existing model that was trained on a very large data set and fine-tuning it? Or do you mean a brand newly introduced model that’s designed to learn only from that small data set?

According to recent reports, ng: Let me describe what Landing AI does. When doing visual inspection for manufacturers, we often use our own flavor of RetinaNet. It is a pretrained model. Having mentioned that, the pretraining is a small piece of the puzzle. What’s a bigger piece of the puzzle is providing tools that enable the manufacturer to pick the right set of images [to use for fine-tuning] and label them in a consistent way. There’s a very practical problem we’ve seen spanning vision, NLP, and speech, where even human annotators don’t agree on the appropriate label. For substantial data applications, the common response has been: If the data is noisy, let’s just get a lot of data and the algorithm will average over it. But if you can develop tools that flag where the data’s inconsistent and give you a very targeted way to improve the consistency of the data, that turns out to be a more efficient way to get a high-performing system.

“Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.” —Andrew Ng.

Recent findings suggest that for example, if you have 10,000 images where 30 images are of one class, and those 30 images are labeled inconsistently, one of the things we do is build tools to draw your attention to the subset of data that’s inconsistent. So you can very quickly relabel those images to be more consistent, and this leads to improvement in performance.

Could this focus on high-quality data help with bias in data sets? If you’re able to curate the data more before training?

In a recent development, ng: Very much so. Many researchers have pointed out that biased data is one factor among many leading to biased systems. There have been many thoughtful efforts to engineer the data. At the NeurIPS workshop, Olga Russakovsky gave a really nice talk on this. At the main NeurIPS conference, I also really enjoyed Mary Gray’s presentation, which touched on how data-centric AI is one piece of the solution, but not the entire solution. Newly introduced tools like Datasheets for Datasets also seem like an vital piece of the puzzle.

One of the powerful tools that data-centric AI gives us is the ability to engineer a subset of the data. Imagine training a machine-learning system and finding that its performance is okay for most of the data set, but its performance is biased for just a subset of the data. If you try to change the whole neural network architecture to improve the performance on just that subset, it’s quite difficult. But if you can engineer a subset of the data you can address the problem in a much more targeted way.

When you talk about engineering the data, what do you mean exactly?

Industry observers note that ng: In AI, data cleaning is vital, but the way the data has been cleaned has often been in very manual ways. In computer vision, someone may visualize images through a Jupyter notebook and maybe spot the problem, and maybe fix it. But I’m excited about tools that allow you to have a very large data set, tools that draw your attention promptly and efficiently to the subset of data where, say, the labels are noisy. Or to quickly bring your attention to the one class among 100 classes where it would benefit you to collect more data. Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.

For example, I once figured out that a speech-recognition system was performing poorly when there was car noise in the background. Knowing that allowed me to collect more data with car noise in the background, rather than trying to collect more data for everything, which would have been expensive and slow.

What about using synthetic data, is that often a good solution?

Ng: I think synthetic data is an important tool in the tool chest of data-centric AI. At the NeurIPS workshop, Anima Anandkumar gave a great talk that touched on synthetic data. I think there are important uses of synthetic data that go beyond just being a preprocessing step for increasing the data set for a learning algorithm. I’d love to see more tools to let developers use synthetic data generation as part of the closed loop of iterative machine learning development.

Do you mean that synthetic data would allow you to try the model on more data sets?

In a recent development, ng: Not really. Here’s an example. Let’s say you’re trying to detect defects in a smartphone casing. There are many different types of defects on smartphones. It could be a scratch, a dent, pit marks, discoloration of the material, other types of blemishes. If you train the model and then find through error analysis that it’s doing well overall but it’s performing poorly on pit marks, then synthetic data generation allows you to address the problem in a more targeted way. You could generate more data just for the pit-mark category.

Sources indicate that “In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models.” —Andrew Ng.

According to recent reports, synthetic data generation is a very powerful tool, but there are many simpler tools that I will often try first. Such as data augmentation, improving labeling consistency, or just asking a factory to collect more data.

In a recent development, to make these complications more concrete, can you walk me through an example? When a company approaches Landing AI and says it has a problem with visual inspection, how do you onboard them and work toward deployment?

Ng: When a customer approaches us we usually have a conversation about their inspection problem and look at a few images to verify that the problem is feasible with computer vision. Assuming it is, we ask them to upload the data to the LandingLens platform. We often advise them on the methodology of data-centric AI and help them label the data.

One of the foci of Landing AI is to empower manufacturing companies to do the machine learning work themselves. A lot of our work is making sure the software is fast and easy to use. Through the iterative process of machine learning development, we advise customers on things like how to train models on the platform, when and how to improve the labeling of data so the performance of the model improves. Our training and software supports them all the way through deploying the trained model to an edge device in the factory.

How do you deal with changing needs? If products change or lighting conditions change in the factory, can the model keep up?

Sources indicate that ng: It varies by manufacturer. There is data drift in many contexts. But there are some manufacturers that have been running the same manufacturing line for 20 years now with few changes, so they don’t expect changes in the next five years. Those stable environments make things easier. For other manufacturers, we provide tools to flag when there’s a significant data-drift issue. I find it really crucial to empower manufacturing customers to correct data, retrain, and patch the model. Because if something changes and it’s 3 a.m. in the United States, I want them to be able to adapt their learning algorithm right away to maintain operations.

In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion consumers. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models. The challenge is, how do you do that without Landing AI having to hire 10,000 machine learning specialists?

So you’re saying that to make it scale, you have to empower customers to do a lot of the training and other work.

Ng: Yes, exactly! This is an industry-wide problem in AI, not just in manufacturing. Look at health care. Every hospital has its own slightly different format for electronic health records. How can every hospital train its own custom AI model? Expecting every hospital’s IT personnel to invent fresh neural-network architectures is unrealistic. The only way out of this dilemma is to build tools that empower the customers to build their own models by giving them tools to engineer the data and express their domain knowledge. That’s what Landing AI is executing in computer vision, and the field of AI needs other teams to execute this in other domains.

Is there anything else you think it’s crucial for people to understand about the work you’re doing or the data-centric AI movement?

Ng: In the last decade, the biggest shift in AI was a shift to deep learning. I think it’s quite possible that in this decade the biggest shift will be to data-centric AI. With the maturity of today’s neural network architectures, I think for a lot of the practical applications the bottleneck will be whether we can efficiently get the data we need to develop systems that work well. The data-centric AI movement has tremendous energy and momentum across the whole community. I hope more researchers and developers will jump in and work on it.

This article appears in the April 2022 print glitch as “Andrew Ng, AI Minimalist.”.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Alarms are one of the most important iPhone features, and iOS 27 offers a key feature that should help your alarm actually wake you: a new volume setting for alarms that’s independent of other volume settings.
  • Sources indicate that have you ever accidentally slept through an alarm?
  • Industry observers note that I suspect that’s a pretty common reason for missed alarms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alarms are one of the most important iPhone features, and iOS 27 offers a key feature that should help your alarm actually wake you: a new volume setting for alarms that’s independent of other volume settings.

Sources indicate that have you ever accidentally slept through an alarm? We’ve all done it. And most often for me, it’s because my alarm volume was unintentionally set to a very low level.

Industry observers note that I suspect that’s a pretty common reason for missed alarms. And in iOS 27, Apple finally has the fix—but it requires manually setting up.

Inside Settings ⇾ Sounds & Haptics, you can now set a volume for alarms that’s independent from the systemwide ringtone setting.

iOS 27 has two new sections in this Settings screen: Alarms and Timers, and Alerts and System Sounds. Both include ‘Match Ringtone Volume’ toggles that are on by default. This means your volume for alarms, timers, alerts, and other system sounds are all determined by the ringtone volume.

But if you disable the Alarms and Timers toggle, you’ll get a new volume slider that applies only to those system functions, and won’t be impacted by your ringtone volume.

As seen above, this means you can crank the Alarms and Timers volume up to the maximum level without making every other system sound, including notifications and phone calls, be similarly deafening.

So the next time you sleep through your alarm, it won’t be because the alarm was too quiet.

In case you missed it, iOS 26 introduced a welcome feature that lets you set custom snooze durations for alarms, and also an option to have alarms trigger on your iPhone even if you’re wearing an Apple Watch.

In a recent development, do you blueprint to set a custom volume setting for alarms in iOS 27? Let us know in the comments.

This year the sale is especially good, because not only have excellent older Garmin watches like the Forerunner 265 and Forerunner 965 returned to their lowest-ever price, but the latest Garmin watches like the Fenix 9 and Forerunner 170 have also been significantly discounted for the first time.

I've been testing Garmin watches for a decade and I think the only watch I can't find a deal on right now is the Enduro 4, but even there you don't have to worry, because the almost equally good Enduro 3 is down to $699 at Amazon.

I’ve picked out 17 deals on the best Garmin watches available right now, from cheaper Forerunner models all the way up to the Garmin Fenix 8 Pro, which is $849 in the Amazon sale and still a better buy than the Fenix 9 in the sale, in my opinion.

Recent findings suggest that I think the Forerunner 70 is the best beginner running watch available, and it actually has all the features runners of all levels really need. It's accurate and comfortable to wear 24/7 thanks to its small design, and this is the first time it's dropped under $200 on sale.

The Forerunner 165 is the predecessor to the Forerunner 70 and Forerunner 170 watches, and a good pick, especially for latest runners. This is one of the few Garmin deals I'm a little disappointed by this Black Friday, though, because the Forerunner 165 has dropped as low as $129 in the past.

Industry observers note that the Forerunner 170 has a few extra features compared to the Forerunner 70, most notably music storage, and also comes in this delightful teal color ( which I'd say makes it worth the upgrade alone). It's a great running watch and is getting its first significant discounts this Black Friday.

Industry observers note that this is the biggest percentage discount I've seen on a Garmin watch right now, and it makes the Instinct 3 AMOLED a strong, adventurous alternative to the Fenix and Enduro. It offers incredible battery life and a distinctive, rugged design, as well as reliable sports tracking, but it does lack the maps you get on pricier models.

This is one of the best deals going on for a Garmin right now, because even though the Forerunner 265 is an older watch, it's still an excellent multisport tracker with a bright AMOLED display. It even comes in two sizes and I'd say the only watch that can rival it for this price is the Coros Pace 4.

In a recent development, the Vivoactive 6 is an attractive smartwatch with impressive sports tracking credentials. It has dropped as low as $229 in the past, so a better deal might be yet to come on the watch this Black Friday, but this is still a good price on a well-rounded watch.

Recent findings suggest that the Forerunner 965 is the best alternative to newer top models like the Forerunner 970 and even the Fenix lineup if you're looking for value this Black Friday. It has brilliant sports tracking and navigation features, and a thin, lightweight design. You'll be hard-pressed to find a better watch from any brand for $449.

The Garmin Venu 4 combines its attractive, smartwatch-style design with Garmin's excellent sports tracking, and even as a marathoner, I prefer it to the more sports-focused Forerunner 570, partly because it has a built-in flashlight.

In a recent development, I don't think the Forerunner 570 offers better value than the Venu 4 or Forerunner 965 at the same price, but it does have some more striking design options than those watches, which might tempt you ot pick it up instead. It's a great sports tracker, of course, but lacks maps and a flashlight.

According to recent reports, the Venu X1 stands out from other Garmins thanks to its ultra-thin design, but even though it looks like a smartwatch, it's actually packed with the same brilliant sports and navigation features as you get on the Forerunner 970. At $300 off, it might be the sleeper hit of the sales.

The Epix Pro is the value alternative to the latest Fenix watches, but I'm a little disappointed it hasn't dropped to a lower price than this, because it has been as cheap as $499 in the past.

Industry observers note that I rate the Garmin Forerunner 970 as the best overall sports watch on the market, so getting any kind of discount on it is welcome, and this is a return to the lowest price it's ever been available. It has all of Garmin's top sports tracking and training analysis features, plus maps, all in a lightweight, durable design.

In a recent development, this is a good price for a great adventure watch if you prefer a MIP display, but the fact that the Fenix 7 Pro has been superseded by three rounds of Fenixes at this point makes me hope there might still be better deals to come. If not, this is still worth looking at as the cheapest titanium Garmin watch with maps and a MIP display on sale.

Industry observers note that I've just tested the Garmin Enduro 4 and I'd say the Enduro 3 is the better value buy for sure, because it has all the same key features as the new watch for $200 less on sale. Those features include the longest battery life of any Garmin, thanks to the Enduro 4's MIP display and solar panels.

According to recent reports, the Fenix 8 has now been superseded by the Fenix 8 Pro and Fenix 9, but I think it's still worth considering because it's cheaper than those watches on sale. You don't get the connectivity features available on newer Fenixes, but otherwise the Fenix 8 matches up well with regard to its core features, and it's also a little thinner than the upcoming models.

The upcoming Fenix 9 Pro has a few upgrades over the Fenix 8 Pro, including an all-titanium case, and is also on sale, but the Fenix 8 Pro is still a savvier buy thanks to this $350 saving, in my opinion. It has LTE and satellite connectivity on top of its outstanding sports tracking and navigation features, and is $150 less than the Fenix 9 Pro right now on sale.

It has been revealed that all models of the Garmin Fenix 9 are reduced by at least $100 for Black Friday, including the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro with InReach, which is the watch I'm using as my main tracker right now. If you want the latest and greatest Garmin watch, this is the time to buy it, because it's the first time it's been discounted anywhere.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that 40 Years ago, the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles made their debut. The stars of a black-and-white indie comic by Kevin Eastman and Peter Laird, the quartet of reptilian martial artists were an instant sensation, and within a few years they were the stars of the silver screen, the small screen, and toy stores everywhere. But they've never abandoned their comic book roots: IDW now holds the rights to publish TMNT comics, and after two high-profile runs by writers Jason Aaron and Gene Luen Yang, they're headed in a new, grittier direction.

In a recent development, the Turtles are in good hands. Starting with January's Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles #25, the series will be penned by Matthew Rosenberg, who's written Punisher, Batman, and Spawn, as well as the indie crime comic 4 Kids Walk Into a Bank, while Juann Cabal, a veteran of Guardians of the Galaxy, Spider-Man, and Black Panther, will handle art duties. With TMNT #25 hitting store shelves on January 13, 2027, the last day to reserve a copy at your local comic shop is Monday, November 30.

In a recent development, for a taste of the series' new direction, Collider sat down with Rosenberg to talk about good guys, bad guys, the Turtles' New York City stomping grounds, and the incredible artwork of Juann Cabal. We also have an exclusive look at three preview pages from concern #25, which kicks off "War All the Time," an arc that will see the Turtles face off against an army of their deadliest foes. Rosenberg is a longtime fan of both the Turtles and the independent ethos that gave rise to them. When the opportunity came to contribute to their ongoing mythos, Rosenberg jumped at the chance:.

Industry observers note that "I fell in love with the Turtles as a small child. The bullies who ran my local comic shop wouldn’t sell me the books I wanted unless I bought the reprints of the original Kevin Eastman and Peter Laird black & white comics. Those books rewired my brain and changed the way I felt about comics completely. They were funnier, angrier, weirder, darker, and just cooler than anything else I’d ever read. So when the folks at IDW asked me if I had any interest I could not have screamed ‘yes’ any faster. Part of the beauty of making comics like this is being a part of the legacy, adding a few stitches to the tapestry that goes back years and will go on after you die. So for this book, these characters who really made me fall in love with different types of comics and stories, taught me what independent art was, and just generally told me it’s cool to be yourself, there is no other book I’d rather be writing.".

"War All the Time" is going to pit the TMNT against a bevy of bad guys, in a story that Rosenberg likens to a collision of classic movie genres. "I really love the old martial arts trope of endless gauntlets of enemies that you see in stuff like Enter the Dragon, Ip Man, or even Kill Bill. Combine all that with the classic people vs. New York City-type stories from the ’80s and ’90s like The Warriors, Death Wish, and After Hours, and I think you have something that speaks to the Turtles because all that stuff was originally in their DNA.".

Rosenberg is from New York City, a relative rarity among TMNT writers, and he wants to give the tales of the TMNT a sense of authenticity: "I don’t want to speak ill of other creative teams who have worked on the franchise before, but sometimes it looks like they’re eating pizza from chain restaurants. Sometimes it feels like they only ever hang out in Midtown. Honestly, if all I contribute to the legacy of this franchise is having them argue about which train line to get on, I feel like I’ve done my city proud.".

In a recent development, four teams, four completely different reasons to put yourself in danger for strangers. This is the roster you actually belong on, what they would want from you, and what it would cost you to stay.

Sources indicate that you belong where the stakes are largest and the personalities are loudest. This is a team of people who are all used to being the most vital person in the room, which is exactly why it works and exactly why it keeps nearly falling apart.

Sources indicate that you have never had the luxury of being thanked for this. The X-Men protect a world that has never once been comfortable with them existing, and something in you understands exactly why they keep doing it anyway.

Industry observers note that you do not want colleagues, you want your people. The Titans are the team where the friendship came first and the world-saving turned up afterwards as an inconvenient side effect.

You are not asking who to trust. You worked out the answer a while ago and it was nobody in a cape. This is where you go once you have decided the people in charge need watching, and that nobody else is going to do it.

Capturing the group dynamic of the Turtles is key to a successful TMNT run, as four very different personalities bounce off each other. Rosenberg knows it's a challenge, but is confident in his ability to put the Turtles through their paces while mixing fantasy with reality:.

Industry observers note that "There have been so many amazing iterations and takes, I don’t feel like it’s my job to reinvent the wheel. I’m taking the pieces I really love — the family dynamic of the four brothers, the youthful energy they have, and their wildly contrasting personalities and putting them in a bit of a pressure cooker. We all have best friends we love and care about. But how do we feel when they keep making jokes while we’re trapped with them on an out-of-control 1 train full of killer mutants with weapons? What do you do when the smartest member of your family comes up with a strategy that you don’t think you can all survive? I think what works about the Turtles for all these years is the mix of the incredibly relatable and the wildly surreal, so we’re trying to push both as far as we can.".

Who will they be facing off with? Rosenberg notes that the sheer number of foes makes it less about "who" than "how many," but does note his fondness for one of the team's earliest foes, in his earliest incarnation: the enigmatic, sewer-dwelling, rodent-controlling Rat King, calling him "one of the most unnerving and perfect antagonists.".

Sources indicate that rosenberg also offered praise for his collaborator, Juann Cabal, predicting that he'll go down as "one of the all-time great TMNT artists." He thought the book needed three things from its artist: "1 — An artist who could do action so good audiences wouldn’t even notice if there was dialogue. 2 — character moments and acting so honest that people would forget not just that they were reading a comic, but that they were reading a comic about giant talking turtles. 3 — They needed to look cool." Cabal effortlessly accomplished all three, which you can see for yourself when Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles #25 hits shelves on January 13.

Recent findings suggest that 4 Kids Walk Into a Bank, a crime thriller comic book miniseries by Rosenberg and artist Tyler Boss, first hit shelves in 2016. It centers around a young girl who discovers that her father is planning to rob a bank, and then decides to disrupt his plans by robbing the bank herself. Now, it's going to be a major motion picture, directed by Frankie Shaw (SMILF), adapted for the screen by Rosenberg, and starring Liam Neeson (Schindler's List), Talia Ryder (West Side Story), Whitney Peak (The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping), Jack Dylan Grazer (It), Deacon Phillippe (Motorheads), and Teresa Palmer (The Fall Guy).

Sources indicate that ​​​​​​​Rosenberg calls the movie "a throwback to a type of movie I feel like they don’t make as much anymore. A coming-of-age story for screw-ups." He has great praise for Shaw and the film's cast, and thinks that "audiences deserve to see more kids doing crime. It’s good for the soul.".

Latest Update: MagSafe Monday: Anker’s MagGo Pro 2 has a built-in fan to keep 25W Qi2.2 charging from slowing down

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (711 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The biggest matter with Qi 2.2 on MagSafe batteries is the slowdown caused by heat.
  • MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.
  • It has been revealed that heat is the enemy of MagSafe charging, which is why it slows to a crawl on a hot day and why most MagSafe batteries can’t hold their top speed for an entire charge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The biggest matter with Qi 2.2 on MagSafe batteries is the slowdown caused by heat. It doesn’t matter if the battery specs say it can charge at Qi2.2 speeds if the heat slows it down after 15 minutes. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro directly targets heat with a built-in fan in the MagSafe battery.

MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

It has been revealed that heat is the enemy of MagSafe charging, which is why it slows to a crawl on a hot day and why most MagSafe batteries can’t hold their top speed for an entire charge. Anker’s answer in the MagGo 2 Pro is a small fan inside of it. Anker says it keeps the charging surface below 96.8°F, and the fan adjusts its speed based on what’s plugged in and how the charge is progressing. You can switch between Cool and Silent modes if you don’t want to hear it running at all.

Sources indicate that the result of having this fan is a Qi2.2 power bank that actually reaches Qi2.2 speeds for a full charge. Anker rates it at 25% on an iPhone 17 Pro in 10 minutes, then to 50% in 25 minutes, which is the kind of speed you’d normally expect from a wired charging session.

The MagGo 2 Pro battery is 10,000mAh, which is enough for a little over one full charge of an iPhone Pro Max and closer to two on a standard iPhone. Size-wise, it has about the same footprint as the iPhone itself and is roughly an ounce lighter than Anker’s standard MagGo. It’s not a slim battery, but for one with a fan, it’s workable in your travel bag, crossbody, etc.

The single USB-C port works both directions at up to 45 watts. If you plug in a 45-watt charger to it, the MagGo 2 Pro can charge from empty to 80% in under an hour. The same port will charge a Mac or an iPad up to 45 watts in a pinch, which is a nice add-on for a MagSafe battery. You are not going to charge up your MacBook Pro from zero to full with it, but it’s a nice way to get a little charge in an emergency at the airport, etc.

One thing to know before you buy: the cable in the box is a 1-foot USB-C-to-USB-C cable, and Anker notes that reaching the full 45-watt recharge speed requires a 45-watt-rated cable. So keep that in mind as you pack for a trip.

Recent findings suggest that anker put a small display on the side that cycles through six screens with a side button: charging wattage, battery percentage, battery health, and temperature. It’s a nice touch to know you are reaching the 25-watt Qi 2.2 speed.

There’s also a built-in stand that adjusts from flat to 80 degrees and folds back into the body when you’re done. You can also rapidly turn off charging if you simply want to use it as a stand. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro comes in Phantom Gray, Burgundy Red, Polar Night Blue, and Starlight Silver.

In a recent development, qi2.2 is the Holy Grail of MagSafe chargers, but as I stated in the beginning, it’s irrelevant if the heat throttles it. To get full 25-watt MagSafe charging on the go, you’ll likely need something with a fan, unless you’re in colder weather. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro solves that problem with a built-in fan, a handy side display, and a stand.

The Anker MagGo 2 Pro is available on Amazon and directly from Anker.

3 tips for shopping for a mattress for back pain in the Black Friday sales.

I've had recurrent lower back pain for over a decade, so I know how much it can impact your ability to stay asleep all night. If you are a shopping for a mattress for back pain in the Black Friday sales, there's a few things to keep in mind. 1. Choose a mattress with lumbar support Your lumbar region is the curve at your lower back. A mattress with enhanced lumbar support will support this natural ‘S’ shape, comfortably filling this gap and distributing your weight evenly. The Saatva RX, Saatva Classic and Helix Midnight Luxe are just a handful of mattresses that support the lumbar beautifully. 2. Opt for the right firmness It’s a common misconception that when it comes to back pain, the firmer the mattress the better. Instead, most chiropractors recommend a medium-firm mattress as the sweet spot between pressure relief and support. However, those who weigh over 230lb or are back or stomach sleepers might find relief from a firmer mattress. Check out our guide on how to choose a mattress for more advice on mattress firmness.

Advances in sensing, manufacturing, computational resources, and data-driven methods are enabling new approaches to electromagnetic sensing, non-destructive evaluation, and advanced materials processing. This webinar will demonstrate how the COMSOL Multiphysics software supports predictive modeling by coupling electromagnetic fields with thermal, chemical, mechanical, and transport phenomena across multiple length and time scales.The first application we will show focuses on eddy-current thermometry for reconstructing three-dimensional temperature fields in metal plates. Temperature-dependent electrical conductivity alters induced currents and magnetic fields, enabling volumetric thermal inference. COMSOL simulations of defects and laser-induced transient heating will support validation of reconstruction algorithms. Multifrequency excitation will be investigated to improve depth discrimination through frequency-dependent penetration depths and sensitivities.The second application examines microwave-enabled volumetric additive manufacturing of ceramic components. A high-power microwave beamforming array delivers localized energy into three-dimensional volumes, enabling processing of opaque, particle-laden resins. Coupled COMSOL models of electromagnetic propagation, microwave absorption, heat transfer, and ceramic sintering kinetics are used to predict temperature evolution, reaction progression, spatial resolution, and processing scalability. Future extensions will incorporate pulsed excitation, fluid flow, resin viscosity, convection, shrinkage, and solid mechanics.Together, these examples demonstrate how the COMSOL software can integrate multiphysics modeling with sensing, manufacturing, and data inversion. This webinar will present two applications of coupled electromagnetic and thermal modeling in COMSOL Multiphysics: eddy-current thermometry in metal plates and microwave-assisted processing of ceramic-loaded resins. By connecting simulation with practical engineering systems, COMSOL-based modeling can accelerate technology development, reduce experimental iteration, and support reliable scale-up of next-generation electromagnetic technologies. SSH is a GUI framework

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (807 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zydra

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • "One thing about which fish know exactly nothing is water." — Marshall McLuhan.
  • Recent findings suggest that SSH is a tool so ubiquitous that we've forgotten what it actually is: a multiplexed, encrypted byte stream accessible on a cross-platform rendering engine that ships on every laptop, server, and phone on earth.
  • To see just how far you can push it, I've made a microVM with a desktop environment designed from the ground up to render natively over SSH.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"One thing about which fish know exactly nothing is water." — Marshall McLuhan.

Recent findings suggest that SSH is a tool so ubiquitous that we've forgotten what it actually is: a multiplexed, encrypted byte stream accessible on a cross-platform rendering engine that ships on every laptop, server, and phone on earth. A number of terminal protocols have slowly added graphics, clipboard sharing (including images), notifications, mouse support, and more on top of SSH.

To see just how far you can push it, I've made a microVM with a desktop environment designed from the ground up to render natively over SSH. You can try it right now (no sign-up):.

All terminal protocols work on data that can be passed through SSH, so typically, any terminal protocol will extend to SSH.

Perhaps the most ubiquitous fresh terminal protocol is the Kitty Graphics Protocol, which superseded the older Sixel and iTerm2 graphics protocols. It allows for compression, client-side graphical state (via VRAM), and even animations entirely on the terminal.

According to recent reports, graphics alone don't make a complete GUI, though. SSH has protocols that cover all other angles:.

Recent findings suggest that notifications: OSC 99 "Rich Notifications" allow image, text, and body. OSC 777 (our first fallback) allows only text and body, and OSC 9 (our last fallback) allows only a title.

We end up using a similar fallback for many things.

A few tricks make compositing over SSH fast. Firstly, where possible, especially when streaming terminals, we simply stream them as text rather than unnecessarily streaming it via graphics. The compositor's UI framework itself cleverly overlays traditional text over carefully aligned graphics, saving bandwidth. In the case of zydra.sh, this allows us to efficiently stream the entire cloud computer's desktop UI over SSH.

According to recent reports, next, we optimize graphics by sending a sort of "grid" of pixels. Each cell has its own updates, where the previous frame is compared to the current frame to catch and send updates, avoiding having to constantly stream the full screen. Kitty also offers both RGB and RGBA, and so by removing transparency where it's not needed, we save another 25% in bandwidth. We also track ping and other factors to determine how well the client handles the stream: lowering the resolution in select cells, especially when scrolling, to relieve pressure. We also use Kitty's client-side state to hold graphics ahead-of-time before they're displayed on screen, as well as holding repeated UI components.

Not all terminals support all the latest terminal protocols, so the compositor must also fallback to older graphics protocols Sixel and iTerm2, and when necessary, fall back to pure textual streaming, using ASCII to replicate some UI. In the case of notifications and other protocols, multiple protocols similarly exist, which we also gracefully fallback to when needed.

In a recent development, parsing terminal versions and querying capabilities allows us to get an idea of what the client supports. We also continually verify that features work as expected on the client as the session boots. The Kitty terminal itself I've found to have very reliable support for all graphics protocols zydra.sh relies on.

VNC is limited to sending pictures of the screen and diffing frames to find what changed. With zydra.sh's approach, apps directly tell the compositor what changed, and terminal text is sent as text you can select and copy natively. The browser is a WebKit build that delivers frames to the compositor as DMA-BUFs without a readback, which can be driven agentically via Playwright.

While webapps have advantages, especially in client-side state, WASM, and WebGPU, they don't really capture the universality and ease-of-use of an SSH session. SSH keys double as authentication, and -A allows you to SSH into servers from within a remote microVM itself. Webapps also can't be accessed from a pure TTY.

SSH also has sshfs, so you can mount your VM's filesystem locally:.

On Android, SSH is technically "available" through Termux, although it can be finicky. I've made a webapp version of the zydra.sh compositor that's more responsive and accessible in mobile for this use case.

SSH also still poses limits around audio (as agents are increasingly used with dictation), and despite how much the Kitty graphics protocol helps, it leaves a lot of optimization on the table due to a lack of stronger client-side state and streaming protocols.

My SSH-native compositing system and microVM desktop environment based on it are the backbone of my broader attempt to create an actually pleasant agent sandbox :). A cloud computer without cloud friction if you will. Another article which describes how I added a "timeline" feature to zydra.sh that allows you to rewind the VM as if watching a livestream is available here: Agents need an undo button. You can read more about me and my background on my portfolio, too.

As Black Friday deals are here, it's a great time to upgrade: Walmart has discounted the Beats Solo 4 by more than 50% to $99.95 (originally $199.95); the sale applies to the black, pink, and slate blue variants.

The holiday shopping season is here, and Apple Watch is always a popular gift. Apple’s lineup includes the affordable Apple Watch SE 3 and the more advanced Apple Watch Series 12.

Here’s how those two Apple Watch models stack up….

In a recent development, the Apple Watch SE 3 is the most affordable way to enter the Apple Watch ecosystem. It got a massive enhancement last year, adding a variety of upcoming higher-end Apple Watch features. It now offers an Always-On display, sleep apnea notifications, temperature sensing, interactive wrist flick and double tap gestures, and more.

Recent findings suggest that the Apple Watch SE 3 offers 18 hours of battery life, though you can stretch that to 32 hours in Low Power Mode. It supports fast charging, going from 0-80% in 45 minutes.

Sources indicate that even though it hasn’t been updated in a year, the Apple Watch SE 3 is a very compelling option, especially for people upcoming to the Apple Watch ecosystem. It’s pretty fantastic that you can get an Apple Watch with key display and health-monitoring features for under $200.

The Apple Watch Series 12 is Apple’s newest smartwatch, and it’s a major update over its predecessor. This year, Apple doubled down on the health and fitness capabilities of Apple Watch with an all-new Health Sensing System.

Apple touts that the Apple Watch Series 12 delivers “the most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable.” In fact, the company conducted a study of more than 1,000 participants that found the Series 12 “achieved statistically better overall accuracy than every competing wearable it tested across workouts and daily activities.”.

Recent findings suggest that with the latest system, Apple Watch Series 12 captures your heart rate every five seconds. Previous Apple Watch models, including the Apple Watch SE 3, take measurements every five minutes. The new Health Sensing System also enables a new readiness score feature, which factors in your recent activity, training load, vitals, and sleep score.

As I wrote in my review, the Apple Watch Series 12 brings some of the biggest improvements to Apple Watch health tracking in years. The new sensing system unlocks a trove of new data along with better accuracy.

The Apple Watch lineup is incredibly strong right now. Whether you’re deciding between the SE 3 and Series 12, both offer great health tracking, battery life, and connectivity. The Apple Watch SE 3 is an excellent choice for people upcoming to the Apple Watch ecosystem.

In a recent development, the Apple Watch Series 12, however, is the best Apple Watch for most people. There are major improvements to the health tracking capabilities, offering meaningful steps forward in what the Apple Watch can tell you about yourself. In the two months I’ve had mine, I’ve come to appreciate the more frequent heart rate measurement and readiness score.

Deploying a payphone on a tiny Pacific Island for fun and zero profit

💡 Key Takeaways
  • For the past few years Australia’s Telstra has run a campaign of “Free calls to Santa” from the universal service obligation funded payphones across the country – It’s a really fun idea and we wanted to replicate it on our network on Norfolk Island where we run the mobile network, but the’s no payphones.*.
  • * There is now a payphone – You probably already guessed this.
  • Those who have seen my office / shed / studio / the HackHouse, know that I may have one or two payphones… But this needed a payphone that could stand the elements and be modern ish.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For the past few years Australia’s Telstra has run a campaign of “Free calls to Santa” from the universal service obligation funded payphones across the country – It’s a really fun idea and we wanted to replicate it on our network on Norfolk Island where we run the mobile network, but the’s no payphones.*.

* There is now a payphone – You probably already guessed this.

Those who have seen my office / shed / studio / the HackHouse, know that I may have one or two payphones… But this needed a payphone that could stand the elements and be modern ish.

The answer, is of course, to use the sexiest payphone of all time; the Nortel Millennium. Featuring VFD display, durable keypad, card service, coin service, no fancy metering line required.

Unfortunately Nortel’s bankruptcy in 2008 meant I couldn’t phone up an account manager, but with the hookup of some guy with a U-Haul van full of Millennium’s in the US and a bit of a road trip, Cody from our team managed to pickup some really clean GTE branded payphones for the job.

Then Cody flew to Sydney where we drove to the house of someone who was heading to Norfolk the next day to explain they’d need to leave all their baggage at home as all of their baggage allowance was to be taken up with the weight of a payphone – Thanks Paul.

Eventually with the Payphone on Norfolk, we needed to get it programmed; for that there’s Howard Harte’s great mm_manager, which, with the aid of a USB modem is able to program the phones.

Sidebar: I also got this working with a softmodem (A fork of D-Modem with some minor tweaks I’ve documented here), so we could do it via straight SIP without the USB modem required – but the USB modem was the easier path.

The Philtel blog post covers how to setup your Millennium if you’re looking to play along at home yourself.

I hit a bit of a stumbling block with mm_manager as the software assumed you were part of the North American Numbering Initiative (NANP) – as one of the literally dozens of people who live outside of America, having to put a 1 in front of the number wasn’t going to fly.

After some trial and error I sussed out what bits on the config files that get pushed to the phone controls this and submitted a PR to mm_manager which is now merged.

We’re also able to set the messaging that appears on the screen, which I’m very happy with the branding on.

We set it for free-on-net calls, so anyone can call any Norfone number without charge and the Payphone tag number.

Industry observers note that once this would’ve been the hard part, I did some work a long time ago with IBM Watson and built some stuff to annoy voters via phone with automated phone calls and capture their human responses and sort them and play the appropriate response. But tech has come a long way since 2019, and this was the easy part of the project.

We setup the payphone to make HOHOHO (464646) a destination that did not require coins when we did the rating table setup when programming the phone.

I’ve got 4 pre-recorded “Norfolk Specific” greetings to buy us time to get everything setup in the background, once these greetings play (each ends asking the caller their name) then we feed into the OpenAI API.

One of the members from our team attempted to ask Santa to write a Python script to iterate over a for loop, while another team member asked Santa for firearms. In both cases it did a good job of redirecting.

All the code for this is on Github.

The phone came GTE branded, so we needed to redo the card with the branding on it that goes around the screen. Two screws and some wiggling later we pulled out the card, and then I badgered my partner into using their day off to design a newly introduced one, with a retro style I really like.

The install was beautifully completed by long-time-reader-of-the-blog Minas from Shield Electrical and Air.

He knocked up a housing to Shield it from the rain and elements and installed it outside the office entrance.

The last step of the puzzle was making the phone so it could be captured by cult game Payphone Tag – I reached out to Alex and gave him the info, and now it’s there in the map for anyone to capture.

So with this now in place, we’ve still got to give it some tinsel and Christmas cheer, and I’ll get some more pics of it in place.

We’re waiting for someone to claim it on Payphone tag, and we’ve shipped 3 of these to another even more remote Island I’ll hopefully be able to share more info on later.

If you’re ever on Norfolk, give it a call.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthropic is launching a new tool for builders called Claude Ship. The new AI feature allows Claude to “review pull requests, fix them, and approve the ones that a team’s policy allows.”.

In a recent development, claude Ship is a fresh product created especially for builders who code with agents. The idea is to make handling pull requests as automated as agentic coding.

Industry observers note that “That’s why we built Claude Ship, available today in beta,” Anthropic claims. “It can review PRs, fix them, and decide what’s ready to merge based on policies each team sets. Teams stay in control of where it runs and which changes need a person. The goal: ship code as fast as teams write it.”.

Claude Ship is comprised of three agents: Code Review, PR Steward, and Claude Approvals.

“Together, they take a pull request through review, fixes, and an approval decision so teams don’t have to manage each step manually,” Anthropic says.

“Developers can try Claude Ship on their own pull requests with the upcoming /ship command in Claude Code,” Anthropic says.

You can learn much more about Claude Ship here. Additional documentation can be found here.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, I write a lot about e-readers and e-ink tablets for Lifehacker, and one glitch I'm constantly grappling with is how to write informatively about a bunch of devices that can be quite different in some details, like build or native firmware, and pretty much identical in others, given that literally all e-ink devices use display technology produced by the same Chinese company. (It's called E-Ink.) The best way to do this is to include more video in my articles, but I've lacked a good way to film hands-free so I can easily demonstrate a device's look and feel—until recently.

I recently got an offer to try out a magnetic neck mount from Telesin, a low-cost option to turn my iPhone into a wearable so I can keep my hands free while filming. It's a pretty basic concept, but well-executed: The band that goes around your neck is made of rubber with a firm but flexible core, so you can easily position it to be longer or shorter or at an angle, and the phone mount is on an extending arm with three joints to give you additional options.

It has been revealed that I haven't had a chance to film anything for public consumption quite yet, but my testing has already given me some great ideas for how I can use it to show off, say, what it's really like to use a micro-reader in comparison to a full-sized Kindle, as I'll be able to wear it to give a more accurate user's point of view. And right now is a good time to pick one of them up, as many of Telesin's phone and camera accessories (including similar models built to handle an action camera like a GoPro) are discounted for Black Friday; the one I tested is down to $17, or 15% off.

This won't be the right device for every filming scenario. Though MagSafe holds my iPhone fairly securely, I found that I would accidentally detach it every time I tried to adjust the shooting angle—once even leading me to drop it. That's potentially bad news, as using it may require you to take the phone out of its case if it isn't MagSafe-compatible. (Mine isn't.) But if you're just looking for an inexpensive way to shoot hands-free video in a controlled environment, it could be exactly what you need.

Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

The best thing you can do is compare the prices with other retailers that have Black Friday sales. If that seems like too much work, you can just follow our Black Friday coverage (we're already doing all the searching and vetting for you). Some other tips are making sure you're not being sold an older or cheaper version and always reading reviews.

Offering support for iPhone and Android’s tracking networks, the new Kodak SlideTag offers the neat added functionality over an AirTag of being able to show your photos and more on an E-Ink display.

The Kodak SlideTag is inspired by classic 35mm slides from Kodak cameras, and is built by the same tech giant, Reto, that launched a keychain digital camera inspired by old Kodak cameras too. The tracker’s E-Ink display is designed mainly to showcase your photos, with storage built-in for up to 12 photos, but also the ability to show lists and QR codes.

Now, that icon might be coming back.

According to recent reports, android Authority spotted several fresh app icons YouTube for Android is testing in its latest beta update (v21.47.483-BETA). These icons seem to be tied to a new feature that would allow users to customize the homescreen icon for YouTube, and includes seven designs in total including two throwback designs. One is the aforementioned retro TV icon used on iOS, which was never on YouTube for Android, and another is an old stacked YouTube logo design.

That stated, it’s very fun to get these throwbacks, and we’ll be excited to see this functionality go live.

Recent findings suggest that the Soundcore Nebula P1i is down to $299 from $399, while the Nebula P1 is $699.99, down from $799. Both offer 1080p resolution and Google TV, but their speaker setups are what make them interesting. The P1i has two 10W speakers that flip out and rotate to direct sound toward your seating area, while the P1's speakers detach completely and can run wirelessly for up to 20 hours. The P1 is also brighter at 650 ANSI lumens versus the P1i's 380, though you'll need a power outlet for either projector since neither has a built-in battery.

Small enough to slip into a bag, the Nebula Capsule 3 and Capsule 3 Laser are worth considering if you want something you can easily take on trips or move around the house. The standard Capsule 3 is down to $399 from $529, saving you $130, while the Laser version is $649.99, down from $749.99. Both offer 1080p resolution, automatic image adjustments, and up to 2.5 hours of battery life, although the Laser model is a little brighter at 300 ANSI lumens compared with the standard model's 200.

Taking movie night outdoors is a little easier with a battery-powered projector, and both the Nebula Mars 3 Air and Mars 3 are designed for just that. The smaller Mars 3 Air is down to $519.99 from $599.99, offering 1080p resolution, 400 ANSI lumens of brightness, and up to 2.5 hours of playback. The larger Mars 3, now $899.99 from $999.99, steps things up with 1,000 ANSI lumens, up to five hours of battery life in Eco mode, and a more powerful 40W speaker. It also has a weather-resistant design that's useful for camping or backyard screenings, though its extra bulk might make it less convenient to carry around.

If you're ready to move beyond 1080p, the Nebula Cosmos 4K SE at $1,099.99 (originally $1,299.99) offers a more affordable way to get 4K resolution. Its hybrid LED and laser light source delivers up to 1,800 ANSI lumens, while its Dolby Vision support helps bring out more detail in compatible movies and shows. You also get Google TV and automatic image adjustments for easier setup, though it doesn't have a built-in battery, so you'll need a power outlet nearby.

At the premium end of Nebula's lineup, the X1 and newer X1S are designed for a more serious home theater setup. The X1 is down to $2,299 from $2,999, saving you $700, while the X1S is $2,799 from $3,299. Both use triple-laser technology with 4K resolution, Dolby Vision, and optical zoom, but the X1S has a considerable advantage in brightness, reaching up to 6,000 ANSI lumens compared with the X1's 3,500. That extra brightness is useful in rooms with some ambient light, but the tradeoff is louder fan noise.

One complication introduced by AI is that it can be hard to know if an image is real or AI-generated.

This challenge extends to AI-edited photos too, which might have key details changed by tools like iOS 27’s Extend, Reframe, and Clean Up features in Photos.

Apple is tackling the concern with its newly introduced Reference Image feature in iPhone 18 Pro, and also through a software enhancement that rolled out in iOS 27.2.

Per Apple, its latest software enhancement adds the following:.

Support for SynthID watermarking to help identify whether an image was generated or modified with generative tools in Photos and Image Playground.

SynthID is a cross-platform standard developed by Google that embeds unnoticeable digital watermarks into AI-modified photos. People won’t see a visible watermark, but anyone who checks for a SynthID marker will find it.

#132402. Industry News: Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras
