Industry News: Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3332 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery.
  • Industry observers note that advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated.
  • The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery.

Industry observers note that advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated. The techniques reveal fine details in the sun’s corona, which is white in this image. The tiny pink shapes seen along portions of the edge of the blacked-out solar disk are prominences, which are extensions of relatively cool plasma that can jut out hundreds of thousands of kilometers into space.

The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing.

Industry observers note that A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse.

In the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out.

Sources indicate that “It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn quickly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are.

It has been revealed that miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona.Václav Široký.

During totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study. In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona.

And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that.

Druckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas, an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one.

An image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly shows Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field.

According to recent reports, he photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens. All he remembers from that day is the rush of adrenaline he felt while trying to find the sun in the sky with the lens’s minuscule field of view and keep it in focus for the two minutes of the eclipse.

He insists that he has never enjoyed any of the eclipses he has photographed. “In fact, I have never properly seen any of those eclipses. You are just watching the screens, making sure that it’s all doing what it’s supposed to do. There are so many things that can go wrong and you can’t redo it.”.

A composite sequence of photographs reveals the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse as seen from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain.

Václav Široký and Miloslav Druckmüller.

In a recent development, despite Druckmüller’s outward tranquility on this Spanish hillside, the stakes are high. Just 45 minutes ago, his group heard from their colleagues in Iceland, where viewing conditions had promised to be better than in Spain. But a vast low-pressure system had clouded the entire sky, leaving all three Iceland teams without a view.

Industry observers note that on the Pico Trigaza mountain in Spain, two postgraduate researchers used a laser to get a rough, initial alignment for the tracking mount of an optical instrument. The alignment was necessary to precisely compensate for the Earth’s motion.

Industry observers note that the corona has been a mystery for centuries. Though dimmer—by a factor of a million—than the sun’s visible surface, the corona is nevertheless extremely hot: about a million degrees Celsius compared to 5,500 degrees on the surface. Because the sun’s nuclear fusion engine churns at the star’s heart, it might seem that temperatures should fall farther from the core.

To observe the faint corona in visible light, researchers must block the sun’s ferocious glare. Specialized telescopes called coronagraphs do this with an opaque disk called an occulter. But because light bends around the occulter’s edges in an effect called diffraction, it must block an area much larger than that of the solar disk to prevent light from spilling over and ruining the images. But doing so means obstructing the inner part of the corona, which harbors the most important processes that underpin the puzzling phenomena of the sun’s upper atmosphere.

That’s why total eclipses matter so much to solar physicists. By sheer chance, the moon is exactly the right size and at just the right distance to completely cover the sun during a total solar eclipse. Because the moon is so far away from Earth, the view is not marred by diffraction, and the corona reveals itself nearly all the way down to the sun’s surface.

As astrocameras recorded spectral data about the sun’s corona, a laptop computer [on table, at left] displayed the phase of the eclipse.

Space probes can image the solar surface in other wavelengths, but those views have limitations, too. Spacecraft such as NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory do see the innermost parts of the corona in extreme ultraviolet light, explains Shadia Habbal, a solar physicist at the University of Hawaii and leader of the Solar Wind Sherpas project. “But it cuts off very promptly, so you don’t see its extension into space as well as we can see it in the visible emission lines” during an eclipse. “That’s the biggest advantage,” she says, of solar eclipse photography.

The European Proba-3 mission, launched in 2024, simulates total solar eclipses by flying two spacecraft in a formation 150 meters apart with one acting as an occulter and the other as the telescope. The instruments aboard that satellite, however, have limitations compared to the equipment used by the Solar Wind Sherpas team.

According to recent reports, when Druckmüller developed the film from his 1999 eclipse expedition, the photographs didn’t do justice to the event’s eerie beauty. He spent countless evenings applying his expertise in numerical image processing in an attempt to re-create in his photographs the sights he witnessed in that Hungarian corn field.

Recent findings suggest that it took two years, but eventually he succeeded. Where before there were dull views of the blackened lunar disk surrounded by the blunt wisps of the corona, Druckmüller revealed the subtlest details of the magnetic field lines stretching from the sun far into space. As his photographs circulated among solar physicists, invitations to eclipse expeditions began to arrive.

Solar researchers Miloslav Druckmüller and Shadia Habbal have been collaborating for two decades and 15 eclipses.

According to recent reports, habbal learned about the images from a Ph.D. student who had seen them at a conference presentation that didn’t credit Druckmüller. When Habbal’s team later published the images in a paper, they misattributed them to another researcher. Druckmüller found out through an astrophysicist friend. “I wrote her a rather disappointed email and she responded within 10 minutes,” Druckmüller recalls. “She really didn’t have a clue.”.

The error was corrected, and within weeks, Habbal and Druckmüller began a collaboration that grew into a friendship. “Milos’s processing brings out details that nobody has seen before, and they tell you a lot about very tiny features in the corona that you don’t see otherwise,” indicates Habbal.

It has been revealed that capturing the corona’s delicate structures means finding a way to show its brightest and faintest features in the same image. “During the solar eclipse, the contrast between the darkest and brightest parts of the corona is enormous, possibly one to a million,” Druckmüller explains. “But a computer monitor only allows you to display a contrast ratio of one to about 800.” (Some modern monitors, particularly OLED ones, can deliver higher contrast ratios.).

The human eye can adjust to this enormous range of brightness, allowing an observer to see both the bright corona and the faint stars and planets that briefly emerge in the darkened sky. To bring those details together in a photograph, Druckmüller uses custom image-processing algorithms to combine exposures that capture different parts of that range.

Researchers Martin Šebek and Peter Urgoš make fine adjustments to the focus and alignment of the astrocameras on a key optical instrument before the 12 August solar eclipse.

Industry observers note that to create a single image, Druckmüller’s teams need to take 200 individual frames during the eclipse at exposure times ranging from 0.001 second to two seconds. The data must then be calibrated against a vast number of reference images to filter out noise and imperfections. Flat fields, which depict a uniform light background, help correct for defects caused by telescope optics, dust spots, and variations in pixel sensitivity. Dark frames, taken with light blocked from the sensor, help correct for artifacts created by the camera’s image sensor itself. “It takes the computer more than two days to process one image,” Druckmüller claims. Including the calibration data, a single finished image requires about 3,000 input frames.

Since 2008, teams directed by Habbal and Druckmüller have traveled to every total solar eclipse, spreading out across multiple locations to hedge against bad weather. About half of the teams return with usable data. For the others, it’s just a short and stressful voyage. For the 12 August eclipse, three groups deployed to Iceland and two to Spain.

The teams seek sites close to the center of the band of totality, where the moon blocks the sun for longest. In Spain, the 12 August band of totality cut across the north of the country; the center line of the shadow passed within 11 kilometers of Pico Trigaza, promising Druckmüller and his colleagues a precious 107 seconds of totality.

Recent findings suggest that but duration is only part of the calculation. Totality on Pico Trigaza will commence 51 minutes before sunset, with the sun just 8 degrees above the horizon. That low, the rays must pass through a much thicker layer of the atmosphere than when the sun is higher in the sky, increasing the light distortion that complicates photography. At the researchers’ camp on Pico Trigaza, 1,600 meters above sea level, the thinner air should help a bit.

An abandoned hut on the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain was spruced up so that it could serve as a home base for the research team recording the 12 August solar eclipse.

According to recent reports, “Iceland would have been a much better place for us than Spain because the sun was higher up, some 25 degrees above the horizon,” Druckmüller notes wistfully. But Iceland’s notoriously unpredictable weather made Spain an essential backup.

In a recent development, if you pack a van with thousands of dollars’ worth of cameras and optical gear and then set out on a 2,351-kilometer journey, you shouldn’t be surprised if you finish the trip with a few striking photographs [top]. The sleeping arrangements for the grad students at the Pico Trigaza hut [bottom] were spartan, but the views were first-rate.Top: Martin Šebek; Bottom: Václav Široký.

Sources indicate that on the mountain, locals have spruced up a rustic, long-unused hut for the researchers, running power cables from a nearby telecommunication outpost and bringing in a water tank. Five Ph.D. students drove more than 2,000 kilometers from Brno and have spent nearly a week preparing the equipment. Druckmüller and his wife joined them two days before the eclipse. They cook on a small propane grill and sleep in sleeping bags on yoga mats. “We have plenty of space here to set up our telescopes, beautiful views, and a roof over our heads,” Druckmüller notes with a grin. “It’s perfect.”.

Recent findings suggest that but even the best equipment and a carefully chosen site count for nothing if the clouds roll in. “So much work goes into the preparations and then, if you end up with nothing, you just feel terrible sadness,” says Jana Hoderová, an assistant professor of mathematics at Brno University of Technology and one of Druckmüller’s key collaborators.

As the moon continues to slide in front of the solar disk, the pesky cumulus cloud that kept everybody on edge begins to dissolve. It’s 10 minutes to totality. The relief is palpable.

Industry observers note that the countdown on the computers that control the cameras has begun. The screens are now showing only a tiny orange sliver, and the evening is becoming perceptibly less bright.

Recent findings suggest that twenty astrophotography cameras, most of them drawing power from a car battery that was also buffering the cameras from any grid instabilities, are pointed at the sun. Alongside equipment capturing the corona’s visible light, the team has built an assembly of eight cameras to detect light emitted by various iron ions that arise in the corona.

Among the optical gear assembled at Pico Trigaza to capture the 12 August solar eclipse was a unique instrument designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona [at left]. Václav Široký.

Those instruments looking for iron ions have been put together with resourcefulness and thrift. A colleague of Druckmüller’s laser-cut the aluminum plates holding the carefully aligned lenses in exchange “for two bottles of whisky.” The brackets and attachments were 3D-printed at Brno University of Technology. The lenses, produced for the defunct camera maker Contax, were bought at steep discounts on eBay. By far the most expensive elements are interference filters that isolate the wavelengths emitted by the iron ions.

Recent findings suggest that around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still.

“That’s something nobody else in the world can do,” Druckmüller says with visible satisfaction. The unique technology, codeveloped with Habbal’s Hawaii team, has already enabled researchers to map the distribution of temperatures across the entire corona and to discover previously unseen structures, dubbed “smoke rings,” in the coronal plasma. The photographs also revealed the boundary region where the solar plasma becomes so thin that its ions stop colliding.

According to recent reports, the optical assembly designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona is outfitted with astrocameras, each of which captures spectra from a different ionic species. To do that, each astrocamera is equipped with a spectral filter whose bandwidth is so narrow—one nanometer—that the filter appears as a mirror.Martin Fornůsek.

“Iron is the most abundant of the heavy elements that we see in the solar corona,” indicates Habbal. “And because the corona is so hot, the iron atoms lose electrons and get ionized. The larger the loss, the higher the temperature.”.

For example, a temperature of around 1.6 million °C is necessary to produce an iron ion that has lost 12 electrons. But only 1.4 million °C is needed to strip an iron atom of 11 electrons. Once it’s in a particular electrical state, the ion retains its specific ionization, even as it travels outward with the solar wind. Each of those ions, whether +11 or +12, emits a different wavelength of light, allowing the researchers to map not just temperatures within the corona, but also how those iron ions spread into interplanetary space and distribute heat. Habbal and her colleagues had long been trying to image those iron ions during solar eclipses. But it wasn’t until Druckmüller entered the picture that they were able to develop the gear and the mathematical techniques to do it.

It has been revealed that with just a minute to go to totality, the researchers begin removing protective filters from the lenses. It’s 50 minutes to sunset, and the waning sun has just begun to light up the clouds above the horizon with the first tinge of orange. Then, suddenly, the evening begins a rapid and premature descent into darkness. Along the edge of the fantastically thin solar crescent, the brilliant orange points known as Baily’s Beads flash and disappear—the last fragments of photospheric light visible through deep lunar valleys. As totality begins, observers remove their glasses. The hot air cools. The graduate students remain quietly and intently focused on their gear.

Druckmüller looks up from his camera toward the darkened plains. Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still. The sky is ablaze with fiery colors all along the horizon where the deep lunar shadow drops off. Venus burns brilliantly in the southwest, a sharp white pinpoint in the darkened sky. The sound of camera shutters suddenly fills the air. Then, as promptly as it fell, the darkness begins to recede, bid farewell with another handful of golden Baily’s Beads.

Sources indicate that the crowd erupts in cheers. The Ph.D. students throw themselves at each other and hug like they mean it.

Recent findings suggest that “The students did most of the work this time, so I actually allowed myself to really look at it,” Druckmüller states. “It was beautiful. Pico Trigaza may not have been the best for science photography, but from the aesthetic point of view, it was extraordinary.”.

The 2026 solar-eclipse team at Pico Trigaza in Spain included [from left] Magdalena Šrotířová, Peter Urgoš, Martin Fornůsek, Miloslav Druckmüller, Václav Široký, and Martin Šebek.Václav Široký.

Industry observers note that but for Druckmüller, this is just the beginning. While other eclipse chasers will race to release their images, he will take his time. He expects to publish the first visible-light images of the corona in about two weeks. Processing the iron-ion images, and uncovering whatever insights they may hold, will take months—maybe even a whole year.

“Probably until the next eclipse in 2027” in North Africa, Druckmüller says.

Who knows? Maybe he’ll even enjoy that one, too.

9to5Mac is sponsored by Sony: Score Sony’s INZONE noise-canceling earbuds for 38% off. These deliver immersive 360 Spatial Sound, active noise canceling, low-latency wireless connectivity, and much more.

Customers will also be able to view the items in their basket in real time so they can keep track of what they’ve purchased and ensure all sales and discounts are properly applied.

When done, shoppers can complete the checkout on their iPhone using Apple Pay.

Industry observers note that iPhone users with select banks can manage their debit card balances directly in the Apple Pay interface. According to Apple, you’ll be able to use Apple Pay to add money to a supported debit card directly in Apple Wallet or when checking out.

In a recent development, this one isn’t really a new feature developed by Apple. Instead, it’s something that should’ve happened years ago finally coming to fruition. Walmart has announced that it is finally starting to roll out support for Apple Pay. Apple Pay is also rolling out to Sam’s Club as part of this initiative.

As of November, Walmart’s roll out of Apple Pay across the United States is complete.

As Apple Pay continues to increase in popularity and prevalence among retailers, it’s great to see Apple continue to improve the experience. Personally, Apple Pay is my checkout payment method of choice basically everywhere I shop — whether that’s online or in store.

How often do you use Apple Pay? What are your favorite Apple Pay features? Let us know down in the comments.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This paper constructs an unconditional, zero-error Las Vegas algorithm on a single fixed uniform classical multitape Turing machine $\mathcal{M}$ that computes the exact complete prime factorization $N = \prod_{1 \le i \le k} p_i^{e_i}$ ($p_1 < \dots < p_k$ prime, $e_i \ge 1$) of every integer $N \ge 2$ given in standard binary representation, halting with probability $1$ over its read-once fair coin flips, in worst-case expected time $L_N[1/3, 105]$ and worst-case deterministic workspace $L_N[1/3, 40]$, where.

$$L_x(\alpha, c) := \exp!\bigl(c,(\ln x)^\alpha (\ln\ln x)^{1-\alpha}\bigr)$$.

and $T(N) \le L_N[\alpha, c]$ means.

$$ \limsup_{N \to \infty} \frac{\ln \max(1, T(N))}{(\ln N)^\alpha (\ln\ln N)^{1-\alpha}} \le c. $$.

Sources indicate that every prime factor in the output is certified deterministically via Agrawal–Kayal–Saxena primality testing and direct multiplication against $N$, with effectively computable constants and no unproven number-theoretic hypotheses. A complete, unconditional, Mathlib-only Lean 4 (v4.35.0) formalization of the entire proof has also been completed and will be released in a companion submission.

This paper and its Lean 4 formalization were entirely obtained by Cogentic (arXiv preprint arXiv:2609.40324), an agentic framework for mathematical discovery, using Gemini 4 as the base model. There was no human interaction other than the initial prompt for Cogentic to generate a full proof and formalization. The Cogentic harness was built by Yang Cai, Vineet Gupta, Yanchen Jiang, Christopher Liaw, Aranyak Mehta, Grigoris Velegkas, and Di Wang (Google Research and Google DeepMind).

#132394. What’s the difference between an automatic and manual espresso machine — and the one an ex-barista recommends

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1559 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomsguide ↗ Open Full Page

What’s the difference between an automatic and manual espresso machine — and the one an ex-barista recommends

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1559 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Coffee can feel like an overwhelming pastime.
  • But the most important difference is the type of espresso machine you buy.
  • According to recent reports, what type of espresso machine is best for you, and which should you buy?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Coffee can feel like an overwhelming pastime. There's so much noise online about coffee — grind size, flow rate, milk texture — that I'm surprised any newbies are brave enough to take the plunge and buy their first espresso machine.

But the most important difference is the type of espresso machine you buy. There are loads of different types of machines for different types of coffee drinkers: superautomatic, semi-automatic, manual, bean-to-cup/all-in-one... the list goes on. Today, let's get to the bottom of it.

According to recent reports, what type of espresso machine is best for you, and which should you buy? I'm using Casabrews, Ninja, and De'Longhi espresso machines to exemplify my points today — and they're all on sale for Black Friday.

Industry observers note that the De'Longhi Rivelia is my favorite automatic espresso machine. It has two hoppers so you can switch out beans if you so please, and it makes both hot and cold drinks at the push of a button (but you have to buy the cold frother separately, unfortunately).

Sources indicate that the Casabrews 3700 Essential is the best espresso machine under $100 (of the ones I've tested). This machine makes delicious coffee, and while you need to spend a little time learning how to use it, it's totally worth it.

Industry observers note that the Ninja Luxe Cafe Mini Plus is like the best of all worlds. It has a built-in grinder and tamping assist to prevent messes, and it has both manual and automatic milk frothing. This machine is great for learning how to be a barista.

Industry observers note that there's one key difference between automatic and manual machines: ease of use. (Size and price also come into play!).

Automatic machines are called that for a reason: press a button, and you get hot coffee in seconds.

An automatic coffee machine selection screen generally looks something like this.

Industry observers note that some machines have upwards of 50 recipes. The De'Longhi PrimaDonna Aromatic ($2,499) offers 38 recipes — some of which I, an ex-barista, had never heard of — including hot and cold beverages. At the press of a button, the machine makes your drink for you.

Depending on price, some automatic machines have integrated milk frothing, like the pictured De'Longhi Rivelia ($1,499) or the De'Longhi Magnifica Duo ($999).

You don't have to do anything. No grinding, no tamping, no calculating dosage volume. As long as there are beans in the hopper, water in the tank, and electricity in the machine, it'll take care of everything.

According to recent reports, automatic machines are ideal if you drink a lot of coffee, but either you don't have time to make it yourself, or you don't want to make it yourself. Both are valid.

But what about a manual espresso machine? Manual espresso machines vary in functionality — some have built-in grinders, so closer to automatics, but some are incredibly hands-on. Let's run through a few examples.

This is the Casabrews 3700 Essential. It's the cheapest espresso machine I've rated highly, and my only recommendation for a sub-$100 espresso machine. If you want the cheapest manual espresso machine on the market, I'd go for this one.

Recent findings suggest that this machine necessitates either a separate grinder or getting your coffee ground for espresso at a local cafe. It comes with dual-walled (pressurized) coffee baskets. While a pressurized basket means it doesn't make "technically" perfect espresso, it's a fantastic machine to learn on, as it's incredibly forgiving.

However, you do need to spend a bit of time learning the ropes. Unlike an automatic machine, you have to do everything yourself. You need to grind the coffee, put the coffee in the portafilter, press "start", and steam your milk.

If you want to get into coffee as a hobby, or you like the routine of making coffee, then I would recommend a manual machine such as this.

However, if you want to make your life easier and you have a little more money to spend, I'd also recommend looking at manual espresso machines with built-in grinders, like the Ninja Luxe Cafe Mini Plus.

As you can see, this machine has a lot more going on than the Casabrews 3700 Essential. The Ninja Luxe Cafe Mini Plus has a built-in grinder (on the left) and tamping assist (also on the left).

Industry observers note that although you still need to put beans in the hopper and adjust grind size yourself, this machine takes a lot of the hassle out of your morning brew. The Luxe Cafe Mini doesn't have automatic milk frothing, but the Luxe Cafe Mini Plus (pictured) does. The Mini will set you back $449, while the Plus goes for $499. Right now, though, the Mini Plus is $419, and the Mini is $399.

It has been revealed that the long and short of it is this: No time to spend making coffee? Just want coffee, stat? Automatic — De'Longhi Rivelia.

Want to learn the art of coffee, and don't mind buying a grinder or getting your beans ground at a cafe? Manual — Casabrews 3700 Essential.

Industry observers note that still want to make the coffee yourself, but you want a built-in grinder? Manual with a built-in grinder — Ninja Luxe Cafe Mini Plus.

Although not as integral as ease of use, size is also something to consider. In general, automatic machines are pretty huge. Here's a size comparison of our three case studies.

Ninja Luxe Cafe Mini Plus (manual, grinder).

Casabrews 3700 Essential (manual, no grinder).

According to recent reports, if you're short on space, the answer's kind of obvious — it should probably be a manual with no grinder. However, you need to remember you will either require a separate grinder or have to get your beans ground at a cafe.

It has been revealed that obviously, though, automatic machines are much larger than manuals. I would only recommend automatics if you're sure you have the space for them — they look bigger and bulkier than the numbers might suggest.

For everyone in between, I'd go for the Ninja.

Sources indicate that obviously, the more features a machine has, the higher its price. In general, automatic machines will set you back at least $1,000 — the only models I've tested under this are the $999 De'Longhi Magnifica Duo and the $999 Jura ENA4 — the latter of which can't make milk drinks. Honestly, what's the point? If you like black coffee, just get a drip machine like the Moccamaster KBGV Select ($270 right now on Black Friday deal).

Recent findings suggest that after automatic machines come manual machines with built-in grinders. This price can range from $3,000 (Breville Oracle Dual Boiler) to $229 (Amzchef Espresso Machine with Grinder). As someone who's tested all the cheapest models and all the high-end models, I would be wary of a machine charging less than $400. I'd recommend machines like the Ninja Luxe Cafe Mini (pictured, $499), Breville Barista Express ($699), and De'Longhi Arte Evo ($699) — the latter of which can make cold(ish) brew!

I want you to answer these three questions.

Industry observers note that the Casabrews 3700 Essential is the best espresso machine under $100 (of the ones I've tested). This machine makes delicious coffee, and while you need to spend a little time learning how to use it, it's totally worth it.

#132389. ‘Steps’ Director Alyce Tzue On “Punk Rock” Inspirations For ‘Cinderella’ Reimagining

‘Steps’ Director Alyce Tzue On “Punk Rock” Inspirations For ‘Cinderella’ Reimagining

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2261 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Deadline

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that for Alyce Tzue, reimagining Cinderella meant giving its stepsisters the chance to shape their own happily-ever-after.
  • DEADLINE: How did you collaborate with the writers to develop this inclusive reimagining of Cinderella?
  • ALYCE TZUE: It began when Riki Lindhome and Kate Micucci had the idea for the stepsisters’ perspective and pitched it to Amy Poehler’s company, Paper Kite, which then brought it to Netflix.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that for Alyce Tzue, reimagining Cinderella meant giving its stepsisters the chance to shape their own happily-ever-after. Netflix’s animated adventure film Steps, co-directed with John Ripa, casts Lilith (Ali Wong) and Margot (Stephanie Hsu) as Asian immigrants in a French-inspired fairytale kingdom, where questions of belonging and privilege shape their search for happiness. Meanwhile, Cinderella (Amanda Seyfried) must also learn to confront her own societal complacency and dismantle stereotypes that her inherently kind nature unintentionally upholds. Here with Deadline, Tzue discusses the film’s unique visual style, reworking a traditional fairytale and bringing in new “punk rock” dimensions. Related Stories News Bono Bowl Review: U2 Delivers Halftime Goods & Hits On Netflix & NFL's First Thanksgiving Eve Game, With A Little Help From Dolly Parton News Amanda Seyfried Admits She "Told A Lot Of People" About Her 'You Can See Everything' Role: "I'm The Most Indiscreet Person".

DEADLINE: How did you collaborate with the writers to develop this inclusive reimagining of Cinderella? Watch on Deadline.

ALYCE TZUE: It began when Riki Lindhome and Kate Micucci had the idea for the stepsisters’ perspective and pitched it to Amy Poehler’s company, Paper Kite, which then brought it to Netflix. When I came on board, I made the stepsisters Asian immigrants to a fairytale world. We started with these pillars and bigger concepts that we wanted to honor.

It has been revealed that one was these outsider sisters who don’t fit into the box of what you would traditionally see as a protagonist getting their happily-ever-after. That does involve race, but also the traditional feminine archetype that’s super soft-spoken and polite, sings to animals, is pretty, and has that face shape you see in every animated movie. We wanted them to find their unique happily-ever-after.

It has been revealed that there was another idea where we wanted to speak about magic as privilege. Of course, Cinderella has gone through a lot of hardship, but you can also ask, “Well, other people in this world have gone through hardship, too. Why is it this one girl who’s elevated above everyone else and has a fairy godmother, a magic dress and all of that?” That was another concept we wanted to speak to.

RELATED: Director Of Netflix’s ‘Cinderella’ Reimagining Welcomes Movie Going Straight To Streaming — Annecy.

DEADLINE: I want to talk more about the Asian immigrant aspect. From a cultural aspect, what did you want to showcase the most?

It has been revealed that TZUE: I grew up in a small town in Jersey, and I was the only Asian kid in my class. It was a very homogenous white community. I was not only the artist, quiet and nerdy, but I also just felt different. Back then, you couldn’t really quite put it into words. You just felt like, “OK, the stories I had to tell and the way that I dress and the way that I understand the world is just different.”.

I wanted the stepsisters to be these immigrants to a fairytale world who don’t fit the archetype, and the kingdom is full of conformists. The writers and my directing partner, John Ripa, really pushed toward the idea of a blended family where things might seem great at first, but then the world gets in the way.

The world treats difference with fear. Lilith embraces her culture in the beginning, but then when she’s rejected, especially after she shares this very deeply cultural story about the snake lady, she rejects her culture as well. You see very little cultural influence in her costumes in the middle of the movie, but then, through the love of both her sisters, she learns self-acceptance, and you actually see the snake motif return at the end. It reflects my own journey of, “OK, I’m rejected, so I reject parts of myself.” Then, as an adult, there’s this embracing of my roots and my culture again. One way is through this movie, to show how beautiful it is.

In a recent development, DEADLINE: There are a lot of distinct animation and personality styles happening between Lilith, Margot and Cinderella. How did you go about developing this?

According to recent reports, TZUE: We always knew that the character styles would be really, really distinct. We wanted to make Cinderella our own, but she’s definitely inspired by classic princesses, whether from Disney or from a lot of the fairytales we had read about. We loved the French version of Cinderella by Charles Perrault, so her style is very French, and the kingdom is very French-inspired.

Lilith and Margot are both contemporary. We wanted the world to be stuck in a historical period to represent, “Oh, these are the old fairytales.” Lilith is inspired by punk rock like Emei, a Chinese American artist who wrote “The Understudy” with Justin Tranter and Olivia Rodrigo, who we have as a needle drop. Margot is also super eccentric and contemporary in that way. She geeks out on frogs, but she probably would’ve liked manga if it had existed back then. These sisters were really fun because we wanted them to be super relatable from the get-go.

RELATED: All The Songs In Netflix’s ‘Steps’: Olivia Rodrigo To Amanda Seyfried.

DEADLINE: What was the biggest creative challenge in terms of putting the movie together?

It has been revealed that TZUE: The creative challenge, honestly, was how much to include from the canon and how much to break the Cinderella story. One canon moment that gave us so much trouble is actually the stepfather’s death. For Cinderella to be orphaned, you have to kill off the father, but to show them getting together, you have to show the father. The interesting thing is that, from this story’s perspective, you want to be with Lilith the whole time. You want to sympathize with her; you want to show how the world is rejecting her. But the moment you kill off Cinderella’s father, you shift your sympathies toward her. How do you stay mad at Cinderella when her dad just died?

That montage, when you see the girls go from being kids to adults, starts right after Lilith is shut in the storm drain and ends when she becomes an adult. You wouldn’t believe how many times we swapped those events around. There were 20 different versions of that at every screening. It’s kind of surprising, a little puzzle piece that you have to treat with a sort of lightness so it doesn’t shift perspective too much.

According to recent reports, DEADLINE: That’s interesting to me, because I was wondering how you would put it together. He dies, and then the stepmom is supposed to be “evil,” but it doesn’t go that way at all. I would have figured that that whole part of the story would be the hardest.

TZUE: Right, she’s not evil, she’s just depressed. We actually did have iterations that explored the stepmother being evil because that’s canon, but it really took a lot of the spotlight away from the sisters. Then you have to dive into, “Oh, it’s because of the mom’s influence that the stepsisters treat Cinderella this way.” That took a lot of real estate and time from the film. To get Lilith driving the story, I think we needed to focus on her and Cinderella.

DEADLINE: What was your favorite moment from the film that made you say: “I can’t believe we did it”?

According to recent reports, TZUE: The ending. You know what all the emotions are driving to. I have a personal proof of whether or not a moment is good enough, especially something as crucial as the ending. If I find myself actually jumping up and down and dancing around the house like, hallelujah, this huge breakthrough moment, if I have a physical, emotional reaction like that, then I’m like, “OK, we got something.”.

It has been revealed that I’m talking about going back in time to the storm drain. And then even after that, the ripple effect of kindness. What that real act of kindness enables the world to do, and where that leads, is a huge breakthrough for us. If we didn’t have that anchor, I think things would still shift for longer. We would still be trying to find the right ending.

RELATED: ‘Steps’ Voice Cast Guide: Who Voices Who In The Netflix Animated Fairytale Retelling?

DEADLINE: Let’s get into the cast. You have a stacked cast. Let’s talk about Ali Wong and Stephanie Hsu and then Amanda Seyfried.

According to recent reports, TZUE: Let me start with Ali, she’s been attached for a long while. She was the first one to join, and it was a no-brainer. We knew that Lilith had to have a spiky exterior, be hilarious and witty, and have a contemporary flavor. Ali Wong was our dream casting, so we went out to her and her only. She brought so much commentary on society and a mature take on a character who’s kind of like, “I hate this kingdom. I can see that they’re biased against me, and I totally get it. I’m going to make jokes about how the prince has been engaged to his fifth cousin since he was born.”.

Then we have Amanda Seyfried, who is just incredible. We valued her so much because she takes on roles and immediately humanizes them. It’s hard for her to take on a role and make it one-dimensional. With Cinderella, especially as a legendary, iconic fairy-tale character, we needed someone who could give her many layers and allow us to sympathize with her as a fully human person. That involves her trauma, her own walls, and her people-pleasing. I thought Amanda delivered amazingly on that front.

Industry observers note that and Stephanie Hsu can do it all. She’s so versatile, and I want her in more comedic roles because Margot is such a boisterous, effusive wild child. Stephanie had a lot of fun with it.

Sources indicate that DEADLINE: Young Mazino’s character is a cute, emo troll. Can you talk about his journey into the story?

Sources indicate that TZUE: Once we broke the Cinderella story, we wanted to have a lot of fun with the idea that we had broken out of the constraints of traditional storytelling and were in a fantasy world outside the kingdom. We asked, “What other fairytale tropes could we play with?” The trolls under the bridge were interesting, and we wanted to have more action in the movie. So because of that, we have this society of trolls that don’t belong in either world, sort of like Lilith. We asked, “Can we make a character who resonates with her predicament, in that he also has emotional walls? Can you physicalize it? Can it be a literal mech that he’s in, like, ‘Oh, I don’t belong, so I’m going to protect myself in an actual mechanical creature’?” That’s where Gef came along.

It has been revealed that we also wanted to make him super unattractive in his troll society, but beauty’s in the eye of the beholder. For humans, he’s super hunky and hot. We have so many talented writers. In the writers’ room, we were spitballing, and people laughed a lot at the idea of a super-hot troll. That’s where we got Gef from, and Young Mazino was perfect because Ali recommended him. We needed someone who had deadpan humor and a deep, monotone voice.

DEADLINE: And you’ve got Daniel Radcliffe as well. You mentioned earlier that it was a challenge of where to stay or stray from the Cinderella lore. How did you all decide to create The Prince?

TZUE: The Prince is a great opportunity to poke fun at some of the holes in the original story. One of the biggest ones was, “Well, how do you dance with a girl so close and then completely forget what she looks like, so much so that you have to fit a slipper on every woman’s foot in the kingdom?” That’s why we play with the idea of face blindness.

According to recent reports, we knew we had to make him a little dumb, so we needed an actor who earns your sympathy above all else. The Prince is so charming and really reveals you that he’s trying his best, but isn’t the sharpest tool in the toolbox. We were so lucky to get Daniel Radcliffe. He’s very picky with his roles, but he knocks it out of the park.

DEADLINE: What were some directorial inspirations you drew from, either in style or in how you shaped the story?

Industry observers note that TZUE: We pulled inspiration from quite a few live-action films. I personally love Joe Wright’s Pride and Prejudice. He tackles the intimacy of sisters so well. Some of those closer camera angles when the sisters are bonding, the rack focuses from one girl to the other, a lot of the lighting on the streets—anything that feels romantic. We also drew from movies like Little Women by Greta Gerwig and Marie Antoinette by Sofia Coppola, which was a big one as well, because she infused the Rococo era with a lot of contemporary flavor and made the whole movie feel so delicious, from the pastries and colors to the pastels. We wanted to go maximalist, and that movie gave us a lot of inspiration.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple's latest flagship smartwatch, the Apple Watch Series 12, is worth the upgrade. With this model, Apple has upgraded the processor, added a newly introduced heart rate sensor, and improved the display durability. It's certainly one of Apple's best smartwatches, but that also means it isn't cheap: All these new features give the new Series 12 a starting price of $399, which only increases if you choose a model with cellular data. However, for Black Friday, you can take up to $100 off the Series 12, bringing the starting price down to $299.

Sources indicate that the three biggest hardware upgrades with the Apple Watch Series 12 are the heart rate sensor, the S11 chip, and Ceramic Shield 2. That heart rate sensor now checks your pulse every five seconds, or 20 times a minute. Apple says the Series 12 checks your heart rate variability 24 times more than the Series 11, and your background heart rate 60 times more frequently than the Series 11. The company is even so bold as to say the Series 12 has the most accurate heart rate monitor on a wearable.

Powering the new heart rate monitor is the S11 chip, Apple's latest processor for the Apple Watch. The S11 isn't only responsible for these new heart rate features, however. In addition to running the same watchOS 27 features as other compatible Apple Watches, the S11 on the Series 12 can run Audio Intelligence, Apple's new suite of AI-powered audio features. That includes "Live Rewind," which lets you see a transcript of the last 15 seconds of an in-person conversation, and "Siri Recaps," which displays summaries of your conversations throughout the day. Finally, the other major advantage with the Series 12 is Ceramic Shield 2. This is a display upgrade that Apple typically reserves for more premium Apple Watch finishes, but this year, the aluminum Series 12 gets it as well. That means the watch should be more durable against scratches and cracks, without you having to upgrade to the more expensive model.

In a recent development, how much you'll save on a Series 12 depends on the size, color, and model. At this time, Amazon is selling certain colors of the 42mm Series 12 for $299, while certain colors of the 46mm option run $449 (also marked down by $100). You can also save on the cellular models as well: The 42mm option is right now $429 (down from $499), while the 46mm model is $449 (down from $549).

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A security researcher has discovered a publicly exposed database containing approximately two billion credentials.
  • The scariest part of it is around 400,000 documents came from separate folders for individual victims, creating a detailed profile with all the personal data needed to “own that person” ….
  • Cybersecurity researcher Jeremiah Fowler states that the database contains a huge array of information, including login details for Tor .onion addresses used to access the dark web.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A security researcher has discovered a publicly exposed database containing approximately two billion credentials. The database was neither password-protected nor encrypted.

The scariest part of it is around 400,000 documents came from separate folders for individual victims, creating a detailed profile with all the personal data needed to “own that person” ….

Cybersecurity researcher Jeremiah Fowler states that the database contains a huge array of information, including login details for Tor .onion addresses used to access the dark web.

I also observed thousands of Tor .onion addresses associated with account names and passwords. The Tor .onion services are generally categorized as part of the dark web, and these credentials could potentially provide access to private forums, marketplaces, communication platforms, or other hidden services. While .onion accounts alone do not imply criminal or malicious activity, it is estimated that as much as 60% of dark web sites host illegal material and illicit activities. This is the first time I have seen a large number of dark web accounts in breached credentials. It should be noted that legitimate organizations, journalists, whistleblower platforms, and news organizations also operate .onion services to provide anonymity and bypass censorship.

But the most frightening aspect of it is separate folders for individual victims containing all of the information needed for identity theft.

Fowler told Wired that this data appears to have been obtained through advanced malware.

Recent findings suggest that the “scariest” thing in the database, Fowler notes, was around 400,000 documents that appeared to come from “more advanced malware” compiling information about individual victims […] that create a detailed profile of an individual and their digital life. “If you had that, you own that person,” Fowler says.

Recent findings suggest that there’s no information about the specific sources of the data, but it seems likely to be aggregated from a range of data breaches. Fowler contacted the hosting manufacturer to have the database removed, but it’s not known how many people may have had access to it.

The best protection is to use a password manager like Apple’s Passwords app to ensure you have strong, unique passwords for each individual website and service you use, with two-factor authentication enabled wherever possible. When given the choice of 2FA code delivery, you should always opt for an authenticator app rather than a text message to protect yourself against SIM-swap attacks.

It has been revealed that in September, Apple held a photography exhibition in New York City to show off the iPhone 18 Pro camera. Now, an image of the Bugaboo Mountains from that exhibit, shot by photographer Jimmy Chin, is included in TIME’s Top 100 Photos.

According to recent reports, TIME publishes its Top 100 Photos list each year. The list showcases the pictures that the TIME Photo Department determines best capture that particular year.

According to recent reports, the essence of TIME’s Photos of the Year, selected by our photo editors and presented below, is the authentic, sometimes staggering, reality captured by photojournalism. Someone was there. A news photographer lifted a viewfinder, pressed a button, and captured an instant happening in front of them.

Chin’s image was shot in Bugaboo Provincial Park, Canada, on iPhone 18 Pro. He explained that a traditional production creates a layer of separation between the photographer and the subject, with equipment, crew, and all the moving parts of a shoot. Shooting on iPhone 18 Pro meant that he could create a more intimate environment, allowing for a sense of comfort and spontaneity that comes through in the images.

Image Courtesy of Apple (as featured in the What Holds Us exhibition).

Chin’s goal was to capture the intersection of human ambition and the pursuit of wonder against the backdrop of a timeless natural landscape.

“The resolution and the sharpness on iPhone 18 Pro surprised me. I could shoot a few inches of rock and ice, or a massive panorama, and trust it would hold at size. That is what this work needed. It also meant I carried almost nothing. In the mountains, everything you carry is a decision. I was not thinking about gear. I was thinking about what was in front of me.”.

Apple’s “What Holds Us” exhibit ran in Newly introduced York City in September, featuring work from photographers Alex Prager, Jack Davison, and Jimmy Chin, with each artist using the iPhone 18 Pro to explore the “people, places, and ideas that connect and ground humanity.” Kathy Ryan, the former longtime director of photography for The New York Times Magazine, curated the exhibition.

Industry observers note that the exhibit is now headed to London, where it will open to the public on December 4, from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. It will also be open from Saturday, December 12 through Sunday, December 13, from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that jeremy Conway — an artiste’s agent, and a titan of the industry with an unerring eye for the stars of the future — died earlier this month aged 87. His client list was legendary, a rollcall that included Anthony Hopkins, Brian Cox, Helena Bonham Carter, Benedict Cumberbatch, Claire Bloom, Greta Scacchi, Noma Dumezweni, Joanne Froggatt, and David Harewood,.

Over 50 years ago, Conway founded his eponymous agency. In 1980, Nicki Van Gelder joined him, adding her name to the shingle. There were just three of them in the office then, and when John Grant joined in 1994 there were nine. “We are now 32!” Grant recently told Deadline of the company that’s now a powerhouse called Conway Van Gelder Grant. Grant confirmed that Conway — “his friend and mentor” — had died on 1 November this year. Conway was CVGG’s principal partner until he retired in 2015. Related Stories News Breaking Baz: 'Bunker' Writer-Director Florian Zeller Takes Us Behind The Scenes With Penélope Cruz, Javier Bardem, Stephen Graham & Dame Eileen Atkins News Anthony Hopkins To Star In Post-Apocalyptic Sci-Fi '2048' -- TIFF Market.

In a tribute penned for Deadline, Bonham Carter, who’s still with the agency, recalled a note she had written for Conway’s retirement party thanking him “for my career.” She meant it. She continued, “I don’t think any of it would have happened if it weren’t for him. He started it all; 42 years ago, I was 17 and sitting in Jeremy’s office on a rather low futon or sofa watching him pace up and down in front of me in mild frustration. He had seen me in a Channel 4 drama playing an Edwardian ghost [1983’s A Pattern of Roses] and was convinced I had something. I wasn’t so sure. I thought I should go to university. ‘Look,’ he mentioned somewhat impatiently. ‘I really am one of the top five agents in London.’ And so began one of my longest partnerships in my life. We did, I think about 20 years together. And I never did go to university. And nor did I ever train.” Watch on Deadline.

Industry observers note that conway wasted no time. He fired off a message to Trevor Nunn suggesting that he consider Bonham Carter for the title role in Lady Jane, Nunn’s film about Lady Jane Grey, the 16th-century “Nine Days Queen”. Next, Conway took Celestia Fox, Merchant Ivory’s casting director for a jolly supper, where he advocated Bonham Carter for the role of Lucy Honeychurch in their upcoming production of A Room with a View.

During this period, Grant remarked, “Jeremy represented several of each cast of the Merchant Ivory Films.” Anthony Hopkins and Bonham Carter both starred in Howard’s End, while Hopkins went on to make Remains of the Day. Cross-referencing the Merchant Ivory catalogue, it’s possible to discern that, over a period of three decades, scores of CVGG artistes populated their films.

In a recent development, I met Conway many times over the years — at first nights, at Oscar-night soirées in Hollywood — and every now and then we’d have lunch. He once explained that, as the son of Colonel Charles Maxwell Orr Sawers, a colonel in the 9th Royal Deccan Horse who served in India and Burma, he knew all about “getting work done and just getting on with it.” I found that comment from Conway in a red Silvine notebook, one of hundreds that I forgot to throw away. The army-brat background, I think, gave Conway that carpe diem attitude, but it was cloaked by his avuncular bearing.

But he was definitely getting on with it when he got his hands on Ted Tally’s screenplay for The Silence of the Lambs. And he was getting stuff done when suggested that the film’s director Jonathan Demme go and watch Hopkins in David Hare and Howard Brenton’s play Pravda, which opened at London’s National Theatre in May 1985. The part of Hannibal Lecter won Hopkins his first Academy Award.

Conway loved actors. I would often catch him at plays well into their runs, featuring thespians that he didn’t represent. He wasn’t out to poach them; he just wanted to watch great performances.

Born David Maxwell Sawers, Conway attended Radley College in Abingdon, in Oxford. After that, he studied drama at the Guildhall School of Music & Drama., which is where he met his life-long partner Neville Phillips, with whom he entered into a civil partnership in 2005. Parts in Z Cars, early episodes of Doctor Who and stage roles followed, but Conway enjoyed watching the likes of Judi Dench, Maggie Smith and Hopkins at the Old Vic rather more than treading the boards himself.

Industry observers note that deciding to become an agent, he joined forces with former Royal Academy of Dramatic Arts-trained actor-turned-agent Norman Boyack. Together they formed Boyack and Conway, where their roster included John Thaw, Sheila Hancock and Edward Hardwicke. When Boyack decided to leave the business, Conway set up on his own, representing Hopkins, Susan Penhaligon and Trudie Styler, then an actress, early on in her career.

Once Van Gelder joined, the business grew. Grant observed that Conway was “definitely one of the first agents in London to represent European and world film actors from various countries. As wide a range as Romania, Scandinavia, Germany, France and India. Notably Jesper Christensen, Lars Mikkelsen — who’s still with us — and Om Puri.”.

It has been revealed that aside from his film, theatre and television passions, Conway loved to cook and entertain, and he would regularly host dinner parties at the weekend, inviting the good and the great of the entertainment world. Grant added that he was a keen gardener and collector of art and artefacts. “He was also an avid reader,” Grant marveled, “and somehow found time to read many books alongside a large volume of scripts. He had an encyclopedic knowledge of plays and could frequently be heard discussing why someone was specifically right for a role.”.

Industry observers note that for over a decade Conway was a board director of the London Academy of Music and Dramatic Art, where he was first in line to scoop up tomorrow’s stars. He was also long associated with Bafta, having been a member for 60 years.

A better-than-thriving CVGG is Conway’s legacy; he always had one eye on the future by partnering with Van Gelder and Grant. How he went to bat for all his actors mattered most. I remember being on the set of Guy Ritchie and Matthew Vaughn’s Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels when Jason Flemyng inched his way over to me for a chat and he was almost in tears as he told how Conway had saved his life by “giving me a career”.

That’s precisely the side of Conway’s character that Bonham Carter reflected on in her tribute to her beloved agent, which I’m posting in full below….

According to recent reports, “I think for Jeremy’s retirement party I wrote a note saying, ‘Thank you for my career.’ I meant it. I don’t think any of it would have happened if it weren’t for him. He started it all; 42 years ago, I was 17 and sitting in Jeremy’s office on a rather low futon or sofa watching him pace up and down in front of me in mild frustration. He had seen me in a Channel 4 drama playing an Edwardian ghost and was convinced I had something. I wasn’t so sure. I thought I should go to university. ‘Look,’ he noted somewhat impatiently. ‘I really am one of the top five agents in London.’ And so began one of my longest partnerships in my life. We did, I think about 20 years together. And I never did go to university. And nor did I ever train.

“Jeremy was my industry parent. He was my champion. And patron. My enthusiast. He was bossy, impatient, and had formidable energy and appetite for all things life had to offer. He had great taste. His house, when I last saw him, was brimful of paintings and objects of beauty. He loved his job and he loved it for the culture of it — the plays, the acting, the life, art, the people. His interest and curiosity was acute.

Recent findings suggest that “Of course, most of our relationship was conducted on the phone. He had a great, handsome, fully resonant telephone voice. He had trained as an actor and would always intone, ‘CON-sonants, Helly!’.

“One of my favorite poets, Mary Oliver, ends one of her poems, by saying, ‘I don’t want to end up having simply visited this world.’ Jeremy didn’t just visit it, he ate it, and he tasted it. He explored, and he made people’s careers and opened doors, and he grew an agency from seed that lives and thrives.

Recent findings suggest that “His legacy and his children are the agency and all those he impacted, people whose lives would be utterly different without him. His family of connections and tentacles of influence over decades in the industry is like a tree with many roots, an old oak that will far outlive us all.

“I think of him with huge love and gratitude. I was all his idea. All his fault.”.

On the eve of Thanksgiving at the NFL halftime show, U2 performed the Dolly Parton and Bono duet, “Torn,” as the country great’s image was projected on screens surrounding the stage.

It was a poignant moment during the show, as the song was the final vocal recording of Parton’s seven-decade career. The track appears on U2’s recently debuted album, Carnaval de Luz. While Parton, who shares writing credits for the song with the band and Snow Patrol’s Johnny McDaid, originally wrote “Torn” around a story of a woman trying to choose between two men, Bono and McDaid rewrote the lyrics around a mother watching her family divided. “You name the location,” Bono told Rolling Stone for U2’s recent cover story, “but everyone knows what it is.… People say in the U.S. now, people are scared to go into Thanksgiving.”.

Parton, who died in August at age 80, recorded her part on the album’s closing track in June. “When she got ill,” Bono said, “she got out of her bed to sing this song. And you can hear that. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that there are plenty of reasons Peacock’s The Good Daughter is so damn watchable. The performances, for one—Rose Byrne and Meghann Fahy are terrific as estranged sisters Sam and Charlotte Quinn. But it’s also a great story, tracing the corrosive effect of a years-ago trauma on the women and their lawyer father (Brendan Gleeson) amid the slow revelation of many extremely dark secrets. If you want more of that flavor of trauma-driven drama with a tight focus on family bonds, there’s one movie you should watch: 2015's Dark Places.

Sources indicate that you want buried secrets? Dark Places has seriously buried secrets. Adapted from the Gillian Flynn novel, the film follows Libby Day (Charlize Theron), who survived the mass murder of her family in 1985. The crime is blamed on her brother Ben, a moody loner whose conviction was based in large part on Libby’s own testimony. For a long time, Libby is financially sustained by donations from people who sympathize with her plight, but three decades after the murders, the money has dried up, and Libby is desperate—so desperate, she agrees to help out a “true crime” club that believes her brother is innocent and is working toward his release.

Like The Good Daughter, Dark Places is anchored by a sibling relationship reshaped by the impact of horrifying violence. Libby and Ben’s experience mirrors Sam and Charlie’s in many ways, including in the way both Libby and Ben carry secrets for years after the terrible events that took family from them. The stories are also both compelling mysteries, slowly revealing the shocking truths behind one horrific night, and ultimately allowing the characters to better understand one another.

According to recent reports, dark Places also explores the insular, suffocating nature of small-town life, and how rumor and gossip become a poisonous presence in people’s lives. Libby, Ben, Sam, and Charlie all have to deal with others' assumptions and revelations that they've been betrayed by those closest to them, leading to powerful resolutions. If you loved The Good Daughter, you’ll love this movie. Stream Dark Places on The Roku Channel or Kanopy, or rent it on Prime Video.

In a recent development, want more stories about family dynamics around secrets, violence, and explosive emotional confrontations? Here are a few more movies fans of The Good Daughter are bound to enjoy.

It has been revealed that there’s no violent crime at the heart of this slow-burn drama—just an explosive chaos agent named Kym, played by Anne Hathaway. If your favorite aspect of The Good Daughter was the relationship between sisters Sam and Charlie, then this movie is perfect. Released from rehab to attend her sister’s wedding, Kym is self-hating, angry, and haunted by a terrible event from her childhood. Her sister, Rachel (Rosemary DeWitt), is welcoming, but has never truly forgiven Kym, and the simmering tension between the sisters and the rest of the family drives a drama that you won’t be able to look away from. Stream Rachel Getting Married on Apple TV or rent it on Prime Video.

Industry observers note that if you really vibed on the Southern setting, the slow-burn mystery, and the exploration of flawed justice in the modern age depicted in The Good Daughter, check out Where the Crawdads Sing. It’s a slower, dreamier rumination on rural life, violence and its cost, and small-town justice, but it hits the same sweet spot in its story about a woman named Kya (Daisy Edgar-Jones) who was raised in an isolated house in the swamps of North Carolina. Accused in 1969 of a murder, Kya’s story stretches back to her childhood, when she’s slowly abandoned by her entire family, leaving her at age seven to survive on her own. Ostracized as the “swamp girl” by the town, Kya fights to live her life and be loved while facing the unwanted—and violently persistent—attention of the murder victim. It’s about broken families, deeply buried secrets, and what we do to survive. Stream Where the Crawdads Sing on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

The Good Daughter is about life in a small, Southern town, family trauma, and the legal system—which makes A Time to Kill the perfect movie to watch when you finish the show. When a Black man’s daughter is sexually assaulted in Mississippi and her attackers—local members of the Ku Klux Klan—look likely to go free, he violently and publicly murders them. Local lawyer Jake Brigance (Matthew McConaughey) takes on the case, assisted by law student Ellen Roark (Sandra Bullock). They face violent opposition, withering racism, and an unfair legal system that echoes the environment in The Good Daughter in ways fans will appreciate. Stream A Time to Kill on YoutTube or rent it on Prime Video.

Recent findings suggest that the Dry might be as close as you can get to The Good Daughter in terms of tone and story. Although set in Australia instead of the American South, The Dry is a story driven by past crimes and buried secrets in a rural setting just like the show. Twenty years ago, Federal agent Aaron Falk (Eric Bana) fled his hometown when he was suspected of the murder of his girlfriend. When his childhood friend, Luke, appears to have murdered his wife and young son before killing himself, he returns to investigate. The slow revelation of two mysteries—one in the past and one simmering in the drought-stricken present—makes this an ideal companion film to the show. Stream The Dry on The Roku Channel, Kanopy, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

It has been revealed that set in Boston instead of the South, and focused on male friendships instead of a sisters’ bond, Mystic River nevertheless nails the same atmosphere of dread as The Good Daughter. In 1975, boyhood friends Jimmy, Dave, and Sean are traumatized when Dave is abducted and assaulted by two men. In 1990, the three men remain connected in their Boston neighborhood—Jimmy (Sean Penn) is an ex-convict still connected to local crime, Sean (Kevin Bacon) is a State Police detective, and Dave (Tim Robbins) is a blue-collar worker still haunted by his experience. When Jimmy’s daughter is found murdered and Dave seems implicated, Sean and Jimmy launch investigations from either side of the law, with Dave’s fate hanging in the balance. The ending is powerfully brutal, but this story of secrets and suspicion will resonate with fans of the show. Rent Mystic River on Prime Video.

CAD images of the iPhone 18e, said to come from a previously reliable source, have shown a rather odd new design for the camera bump.

If accurate, it would represent a massive change from its predecessor, which simply has a single lens protruding without a surrounding bump or plateau ….

In a recent development, the iPhone 17e was introduced in March with a design unchanged from last year’s iPhone 16e. While the camera did get some feature enhancements, including the ability to store depth information for portrait photos, the physical camera design remained the same.

Sources indicate that the current model has a single lens protruding directly from the casing with a flush-mounted flashlight next to it. Engadget reports on CAD images showing a very different approach with next year’s iPhone 18e.

The renders show an almost square camera bump measuring about 28 mm by 35 mm that houses the single rear camera, the LED flash and the rear microphone.

The site doesn’t share the images, but indicates that the camera bump looks similar to that of the M5 iPad Pro, shown below.

It’s unclear what might have prompted the change of design, especially as the site’s Filipe Espósito states he’s also seen CAD models for the standard model iPhone 18 or the iPhone Air 2, neither of which adopt it.

Previous reports have suggested that the only spec change with the iPhone 18e over its predecessor will be performance improvements thanks to the A20 chip.

#132379. Tech Report: How Do You Land on a Moon With Almost No Gravity?

📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2950 w)
